steps.step: Product strategy fit & sanction by Management
steps.entryTrigger: PO received and project handed to PM
steps.exitTrigger: Management sanction recorded and project moved out of Data Gather stage
steps.entryQuestion: Is this product aligned with what we intend to build, and do we have the capability and capacity now?
steps.exitQuestion: Has management sanctioned scope, budget envelope and team, in writing?
steps.whatToDo: Open a new Internal MoM and record the sanction: scope, budget ceiling, timeline and the named person who approved each. A sanction that lives only in a conversation cannot be pointed at later.
steps.guidelines: Test the project against three things before committing resource: strategic fit, technical capability, and current capacity against the other live projects. A project that is technically deliverable but arrives when the hardware team is already fully committed will damage two projects rather than one. Record the sanction with its conditions — sanction with an unstated caveat is not sanction. This is the gate that moves the project out of Data Gather.

steps.exitTrigger: Vision and objective statement written and agreed with client
steps.entryQuestion: Do we know who the end user is and what success looks like for them?
steps.exitQuestion: Can every downstream design decision be traced back to a stated objective?
steps.whatToDo: Create the file and fill the vision block: who the end user is, what problem the product solves, and the three features that decide whether it succeeds. Leave the risk table empty for now.
steps.guidelines: Write down what the product is for, who uses it, and what measurable outcome defines success — in a page, not a deck. This is the reference the team returns to when a design trade-off has no obvious answer. Vague objectives ('a good IoT gateway') resolve nothing; specific ones ('runs 18 months on two AA cells in an unheated outdoor cabinet') resolve most things. Agree it with the client so it is a shared reference, not our interpretation.

steps.exitTrigger: Budget approved and loaded against the Project ID
steps.entryQuestion: Have vendor quotes been collected for the major cost drivers before timelines are committed?
steps.exitQuestion: Is there a costed line for BOM, PCB, assembly, logistics and enclosures, with contingency stated?
steps.whatToDo: Create the budget and enter a costed line for BOM, PCB, assembly, enclosure, tooling, test and certification. Each line carries the vendor quote it came from.
steps.guidelines: Build the budget from vendor quotes, not from memory of the last project. Collect quotes for the major cost drivers first — cells, main IC, enclosure tooling, certification — because these dominate and they move. Load the five expense categories (BoM, PCB, Assembly, Logistics, Enclosures) against the Project ID with an approval line, so actual expense can be tracked against plan per category. State contingency explicitly rather than padding line items.

steps.exitTrigger: Team allocated and recorded in CPTS with availability confirmed
steps.entryQuestion: Is one accountable owner named per domain, and is that person actually available?
steps.exitQuestion: Does any allocated person have a conflicting commitment on another live project in the same window?
steps.whatToDo: Add the resource table: one accountable owner per domain, their allocation percentage, and their other live commitments. Flag anyone allocated above 100%.
steps.guidelines: Name one accountable owner per domain — hardware, firmware, enclosure, testing. Shared ownership is prohibited; two names against one deliverable reliably produces neither. Check availability against the other live projects before confirming, not after: allocation conflicts discovered at execution are the most common cause of silent schedule slip. Record the allocation in CPTS so capacity is visible across the portfolio.

steps.exitTrigger: Milestone plan baselined and shared with client
steps.entryQuestion: Are milestones tied to demonstrable artefacts rather than to elapsed time?
steps.exitQuestion: Does each milestone have a defined deliverable, an owner and an acceptance test?
steps.whatToDo: Create the tracker and enter each milestone against a demonstrable artefact, not a date alone. Every milestone needs a deliverable that can be shown.
steps.guidelines: Set milestones against artefacts that can be shown — schematic release, first article, DVT report — not against calendar quarters. Each milestone needs a deliverable, an owner and a test that decides whether it is met. Align payment milestones with these so commercial and technical progress cannot diverge. Baseline the plan; subsequent movement is tracked as variance against the baseline rather than by quietly editing dates.

steps.entryTrigger: Milestones set and engineering team allocated
steps.exitTrigger: Designer LLD issued to hardware, firmware and enclosure leads
steps.entryQuestion: Is the customer LLD locked, and is the requirement set complete enough to specify to a designer?
steps.exitQuestion: Can a designer start work from this document without asking clarifying questions?
steps.whatToDo: Create the developer LLD from the customer LLD. Add the internal detail a designer needs: rails, interfaces, peripheral map, mechanical envelope, and the assumptions behind each.
steps.guidelines: This is the internal engineering specification, distinct from the customer LLD. Work through the 21-step structure: I/O count with 20–30% margin, MCU selection criteria, module-versus-discrete decisions, multi-source alternates, and the hardware-to-firmware interface definition. No execution task proceeds without both the Customer LLD and the Designer LLD locked — this gate is non-negotiable and holds under schedule pressure. Test the document by asking whether a designer could start from it cold.

steps.entryTrigger: Designer LLD issued and board count known
steps.exitTrigger: Eb-PCB IDs issued for every board and recorded in the ID registry
steps.entryQuestion: How many distinct boards does this product need, and is each one identified?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every board in the architecture have its own ID and revision field?
steps.whatToDo: Record the allocated PCB ID(s) against the project. One ID per board, issued once, never reused.
steps.guidelines: Assign Eb-PCB-[ProjectID]-[Rev] for each distinct board. Products with a main board plus a daughter or display board need separate IDs from the outset — retrofitting a second ID after layout has started leaves two months of files under the wrong name. Record every ID in the ID registry alongside the Client, Project and Product IDs so there is one place to resolve any identifier.

steps.entryTrigger: Designer LLD issued and firmware images scoped
steps.exitTrigger: Eb-FW IDs issued and linked to the corresponding PCB IDs
steps.entryQuestion: How many distinct firmware images does this product need (application, bootloader, production test)?
steps.exitQuestion: Is each firmware ID linked to the board revision it targets?
steps.whatToDo: Record the allocated firmware ID(s) and which board each one runs on.
steps.guidelines: Assign a firmware ID per distinct image and link each to the PCB ID and revision it targets. The firmware-to-board-revision link is what allows a returned unit to be diagnosed two years later; without it, 'which build is on this board' becomes unanswerable. Include production-test firmware in the scope — it is a real deliverable with its own lifecycle, not a script someone keeps locally.

steps.entryTrigger: Project ID issued and PM assigned
steps.exitTrigger: Handover meeting held and PM confirms ownership
steps.entryQuestion: Has Sales attached the client MoM, questionnaire responses, LLD and PO to the handover?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the PM have every commitment Sales made, including verbal ones?
steps.whatToDo: Add the handover MoM: what Sales committed to, what is documented, and every commitment that exists only verbally. The verbal ones are the risk.
steps.guidelines: Hold this as a meeting, not a file transfer. The critical content is the commitments Sales made that are not in the documents — timeline hints, feature reassurances, pricing signals. Surface them now, because they will surface later as client expectations regardless. After handover Sales steps back and the PM owns the engagement end to end, with one named communication route to the client.

steps.entryTrigger: Handover complete and Designer LLD issued
steps.exitTrigger: Kickoff held, MoM circulated, first tasks assigned
steps.entryQuestion: Have the engineering leads read the LLD before the meeting?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every lead know their first deliverable and its date?
steps.whatToDo: Add the kickoff MoM: attendees, the scope as engineering understands it, and every open question with a named owner and a date.
steps.guidelines: Write the plan into the MoM before the meeting starts — the MoM pre-exists the meeting rather than being captured during it, which converts the session from a briefing into a review. Walk the LLD, the architecture and the risk plan. Close with each lead's first deliverable and date recorded. Leads who have not read the LLD beforehand should say so and the kickoff should be moved rather than run hollow.

steps.exitTrigger: All access granted and confirmed by each team member
steps.entryQuestion: Does every allocated person have the tools, repositories and folders they need?
steps.exitQuestion: Has each person confirmed they can actually open what they were granted?
steps.whatToDo: Record which folders, repos and tools each person has been given, and by when. Access granted late is schedule lost silently.
steps.guidelines: Provision Drive folder tree access, repository access, EDA licences and tracker access on day one. Confirm by asking each person to open the thing, not by checking the grant was issued — permission inherited from a parent folder frequently does not resolve as expected. Access delays are invisible in status reporting and show up a week later as unexplained slip.

steps.exitTrigger: Market study documented with competitor benchmark table
steps.entryQuestion: Do we know what already exists in this category and at what price?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the study changed or confirmed any assumption in the LLD?
steps.whatToDo: Add the competitor benchmark table: each competing product, its price, and how it scores against your feature list. Note where you are worse and why that is acceptable.
steps.guidelines: Map the category: who sells into it, at what price, with what feature set and what certifications. Use EXIM data where import volumes tell you more than marketing pages. The purpose is to challenge our assumptions, not to justify them — a study that confirms everything we already believed was not a study. Feed anything that contradicts the LLD back into the LLD review step.

steps.exitTrigger: Reference products selected and justified
steps.entryQuestion: Which existing products are closest to what we are building, and why those?
steps.exitQuestion: Does each selected reference answer a specific open question in our design?
steps.whatToDo: Create the teardown record and list the reference products you intend to buy, with the specific question each one is meant to answer.
steps.guidelines: Select references that answer specific questions — how they solved thermal, what they used for the power stage, how they achieved the IP rating — rather than products that merely look similar. Two or three well-chosen references teach more than a shelf of lookalikes. Record why each was chosen so the teardown has a purpose beyond curiosity.

steps.exitTrigger: Reference units received and logged
steps.entryQuestion: Is the purchase approved and are lead times compatible with the design schedule?
steps.exitQuestion: Did the units arrive in time to inform design, or have they arrived after the decisions they were meant to inform?
steps.whatToDo: Record what was actually procured: source, date, cost and unit condition. A used unit and a new unit teach different things.
steps.guidelines: Order early — reference products routinely take three to six weeks and arrive after the decisions they were meant to inform, which wastes the spend entirely. Raise the purchase through the payment approval route with the project ID attached. Log receipt against the project so the units are traceable and do not disappear into someone's drawer.

steps.exitTrigger: Teardown documented with photographs and learnings captured
steps.entryQuestion: Are the specific questions this teardown must answer written down before we open it?
steps.exitQuestion: Have the learnings been fed into the Component Database and the LLD review?
steps.whatToDo: Add the teardown itself: photographs, BOM observed, construction method, and the learnings that change your design. A teardown with no design consequence was a hobby.
steps.guidelines: Write the questions before opening the unit, otherwise the teardown becomes an unstructured browse. Photograph at each stage — the assembly order is itself information. Record the main IC, power topology, connector choices, thermal path and enclosure construction. Learnings go into the Component Database as proven parts and reference blocks, and anything that contradicts our LLD goes into the LLD review that follows.

steps.step: LLD for developer review once again with respect to market findings
steps.entryTrigger: Market study and teardown learnings available
steps.exitTrigger: LLD revised and reissued, or explicitly confirmed unchanged
steps.entryQuestion: What in the LLD does the market evidence now contradict or confirm?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every change carried with its rationale and impact, and has the version been incremented?
steps.whatToDo: Revise the LLD against the market study and teardown findings, then bump the revision. If nothing changed, write that down explicitly with a date.
steps.guidelines: This is the point where market evidence is allowed to change the design cheaply. Walk the LLD against the teardown and study findings. Every change carries its rationale and impact — silent edits destroy traceability and are the reason nobody can later reconstruct why a decision was made. If nothing changes, record that as a deliberate finding rather than skipping the step.

steps.exitTrigger: Electrical test parameters documented and agreed with client
steps.entryQuestion: What electrical behaviour must this product demonstrate, and to what limits?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every parameter stated with a numeric limit and a measurement method?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the electrical section: every rail and signal, with target, minimum, maximum, and the method that will measure it. A parameter with no tolerance can neither pass nor fail.
steps.guidelines: Define what 'electrically correct' means as numbers: supply rail tolerances, ripple limits, inrush, quiescent and peak current, efficiency at defined load points, ESD and surge withstand. Each parameter needs a limit and a method — 'low ripple' is not testable. These parameters must be set before design finalisation because they drive component selection and test point strategy, not after, when they merely describe what was built.

steps.exitTrigger: Reliability targets and MTBF calculation basis documented
steps.entryQuestion: What is the expected service life and duty cycle in the real deployment?
steps.exitQuestion: Are the derating rules and the operating profile stated, not just a headline MTBF number?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the reliability section: MTBF target, operating hours assumption, duty cycle and the ambient it is claimed at.
steps.guidelines: State the service life, duty cycle and ambient profile the product must survive, then set derating rules against it — electrolytic capacitor life and semiconductor junction temperature drive most field failures in this class of product. Record the MTBF calculation basis and standard used. A bare MTBF figure with no operating profile behind it cannot be verified and should not be quoted to a client.

steps.exitTrigger: Board-level functional test parameters documented
steps.entryQuestion: What must be verified on a bare assembled board before it is fit to integrate?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every parameter map to a physically accessible net or test point?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the board-level functional section: what must be verified on a bare assembled board before it is fit to build on.
steps.guidelines: Define what a bare board must demonstrate before integration: rails within tolerance, MCU enumerating, each interface responding, each sensor returning plausible data. This document drives the test point strategy directly — every parameter here must map to a net that will still be accessible after assembly, which is why it belongs before layout rather than after.

steps.exitTrigger: Unit test parameters and coverage targets documented
steps.entryQuestion: Which firmware modules carry logic worth testing in isolation?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the coverage target stated per module maturity rather than as a single blanket number?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the unit test section: which firmware modules will be tested on the host and the coverage target for each.
steps.guidelines: Define which modules get host-side unit tests and to what coverage — logic-bearing modules such as state machines, protocol parsers and buffer handling, not thin hardware wrappers. Set coverage expectations by maturity: Stable shared components carry a higher bar than product-specific application code. Tests run in CI, not on a developer's machine, or they decay within a month.

steps.entryTrigger: Board-level parameters defined and product architecture known
steps.exitTrigger: Product-level functional test parameters documented and agreed with client
steps.entryQuestion: What must the assembled product do, end to end, from the user's position?
steps.exitQuestion: Would passing every one of these tests satisfy the client's definition of a working product?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the product-level section: what the finished product must demonstrate, in the user's terms rather than the engineer's.
steps.guidelines: Describe the product's behaviour as the user experiences it: power-on to operational, provisioning, normal operation, fault and recovery, and end of life. This is the document that defines 'done' for the client, so agree it with them explicitly. If passing every test here would still leave the client dissatisfied, the parameters are incomplete and finding that out now costs nothing.

steps.exitTrigger: Environmental test parameters documented with standards referenced
steps.entryQuestion: Where does this product actually live, and what does that environment do to it?
steps.exitQuestion: Are temperature, humidity, ingress, vibration and shock limits each tied to a named standard and grade?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the environmental section: temperature, humidity, IP, drop and vibration, each with the standard and severity level it is tested to.
steps.guidelines: Set limits from the real deployment, not from a default table: operating and storage temperature range, humidity, IP rating per IEC 60529, vibration and mechanical shock. Reference the standard and the grade for each. These parameters drive material selection, sealing strategy and component temperature grades, so they must be fixed before enclosure and component decisions rather than discovered during validation.

steps.exitTrigger: Pre-compliance parameters documented against the target standards
steps.entryQuestion: Which certification route applies — BIS, FCC, CE, UL — and which clauses bite?
steps.exitQuestion: Do we know which specific clauses we are most likely to fail and have we planned to test them early?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the pre-compliance section: which emissions and immunity tests you will run in-house before booking a lab.
steps.guidelines: Fix the certification route now — it determines creepage and clearance, insulation strategy, marking requirements and the entire safety parameter set. Identify the clauses most likely to bite for this topology, typically radiated emissions and conducted immunity, and plan to test those in-house first. Late compliance realisation is the classic cause of delay in this business, and it is almost always avoidable at this step.

steps.exitTrigger: Integration test plan documented with sequence and entry criteria
steps.entryQuestion: Which subsystems must prove they work together, and in what order?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the plan state what must already be proven before each integration stage begins?
steps.whatToDo: Create the plan and define the integration test scope now, at feasibility — which interfaces get tested together and what proves the system, not the parts.
steps.guidelines: Sequence the integration: hardware bring-up, then firmware on hardware, then enclosure fit, then full product with cloud or app. State the entry criteria for each stage — integrating before the prior stage is proven produces failures nobody can attribute. Name who signs off each stage. This plan is what turns three parallel design tracks back into one product.

steps.exitTrigger: Additional test parameters documented or a nil return recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Is there anything in this product's use, market or contract that the standard families do not cover?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the client confirmed no further acceptance tests exist beyond those documented?
steps.whatToDo: Populate any remaining test family the product needs, with the same discipline: target, limits, method, and who agreed it.
steps.guidelines: Catch what the standard families miss: client-specific acceptance tests, market-specific requirements, life testing on mechanisms, battery cycle life, or interoperability with the client's existing installed base. Ask the client directly whether any acceptance test exists that we have not covered. Record a nil return if there is nothing — an unanswered question here reappears as a surprise acceptance criterion at delivery.

steps.step: Product Features & Risk Management Plan - What can go wrong ?
steps.entryTrigger: Feature set and test parameters defined
steps.exitTrigger: Risk plan documented with at least one technical and one execution risk per major feature, each mitigated
steps.entryQuestion: For each major feature, what is the technical risk and what is the execution risk?
steps.exitQuestion: Has this been reviewed with engineering rather than written by PM alone?
steps.whatToDo: Fill the risk table: what can go wrong, how likely, how bad, and the mitigation with an owner. Include the risks you would rather not write down.
steps.guidelines: For every major feature, name at least one technical risk and one execution risk, each with a mitigation and an owner. Technical risk is what might not work; execution risk is what might not arrive — single-source parts, long-lead tooling, certification slots, a client decision we depend on. Review it with engineering; a risk plan written by PM alone lists the risks PM can imagine. Every open item goes into the Project Risk Register and is tracked to closure.

steps.exitTrigger: PRD signed off by product, engineering and management
steps.entryQuestion: Is the PRD internally coherent, and does it reconcile cost target, feature set and volume?
steps.exitQuestion: Are cost target, BOM ceiling and volume forecast consistent with each other and with the budget?
steps.whatToDo: Walk the whole file with the client, capture their sign-off, and freeze this revision. Anything they change after this is an ECN, not a correction.
steps.guidelines: Walk the full PRD: vision, personas, functional requirements, non-functional spec, operating environment, power budget, form factor, connectivity, cost target as BOM and COGS, volume forecast, and the risk and assumption log. The reconciliation that matters is between cost target, feature set and volume — these three are usually agreed separately and are often mutually impossible. Sign-off is from product, engineering and management together.

steps.step: Share the Journey Doc with Client
steps.exitTrigger: Journey Document shared and client acknowledgement received
steps.entryQuestion: Does the Journey Document separate confirmed requirements, assumptions and unknowns clearly?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the client acknowledged it in writing, and have they responded to the assumptions?
steps.whatToDo: Issue the HLD timeline and step map to the client. Confirm they understand the sequence and where their inputs block your progress.
steps.guidelines: The Journey Document is the single baseline for the engagement and it must separate confirmed requirements from assumptions from unknowns. Nothing is estimated, scheduled or designed before this is shared and acknowledged. Ask the client to respond specifically to the assumptions — silence on an assumption is not agreement, and it will not be treated as agreement when it is challenged later.

steps.step: Share the Milestone tracker with Client
steps.exitTrigger: Milestone tracker shared and review cadence agreed
steps.entryQuestion: Are the milestones, their deliverables and their client-side dependencies all stated?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the client understand which milestones depend on their inputs and by when?
steps.whatToDo: Share the milestone tracker with the client and agree the review cadence against it.
steps.guidelines: Share the milestone plan with the client-side dependencies made explicit — approvals, sample deliveries, decisions, artwork. Client-caused delay is the most common schedule risk and the hardest to recover, and it is only manageable if their dependencies are visible from the start. Agree a review cadence. Route all communication through the single named channel; direct approaches to individual engineers disrupt the team and fragment the record.

steps.entryTrigger: Design definition sufficiently advanced to identify long-lead and evaluation parts
steps.exitTrigger: Trial BOM ordered with lead times confirmed and tracked
steps.entryQuestion: Which parts are long-lead or single-source, and have alternates been identified?
steps.exitQuestion: Will every ordered part arrive before the design stage that needs it?
steps.whatToDo: Create the BOM in Eb format and mark the trial-order lines. Order long-lead and single-source parts now — they will otherwise set your prototype date.
steps.guidelines: Order evaluation parts and long-lead items now — this is the last serial step before the three design tracks run in parallel, and a part that arrives late blocks the firmware track specifically. Follow the channel priority: Digikey, then Robu, then Mouser for BOM items. Confirm lead times in writing and map each against the stage that needs it. Raise payment through the approval route with the project ID attached. Anything over four weeks needs an identified alternate.

steps.entryTrigger: Project ID issued and board count known
steps.exitTrigger: Audit Checklist instantiated for the project with one checklist tab per board
steps.entryQuestion: How many distinct PCBs does this product contain, and is each one identified?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the file carry one checklist tab and one EMS Requirements tab per board, named to the board ID?
steps.whatToDo: Copy the master Audit Checklist and duplicate the checklist tab once per board in the product, naming each tab after the board ID.
steps.guidelines: Copy the master Audit Checklist and duplicate the checklist tab once per board in the product, naming each tab after the board ID rather than Sheet1, Sheet2. A multi-board product built on a single-tab file forces engineers to overwrite each other's evidence. Do this at project start, not at first review, because the checklist is the exit artefact for every step that follows.

steps.step: Audit Checklist scoping and applicability marking
steps.exitTrigger: Every row marked Required, Conditional or Not-Applicable with a reason recorded against each exclusion
steps.entryQuestion: Which test families, compliance standards and assembly steps genuinely apply to this product?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every Not-Applicable row carry a written reason, and has the PM signed the scoped list?
steps.whatToDo: Walk every checklist row and mark it Required, Conditional or Not-Applicable, writing a reason against every exclusion. This is what makes the completion percentage mean anything.
steps.guidelines: Walk every row and mark it Required, Conditional or Not-Applicable, writing a reason against every exclusion. A simple sensor node should not be carrying mains-compliance rows it will never satisfy. This step is what makes the completion percentage mean something — without it people bulk-fill 'Not started' across a hundred irrelevant rows and the checklist reports progress that does not exist.

steps.entryTrigger: Project sanctioned and engineering team allocated
steps.exitTrigger: Governing DFM and DFT standard received, revision and date logged, and the Elecbits house standard revision fixed for this project
steps.entryQuestion: Whose manufacturing and test rules govern this project — the customer's, ours, or a merge of both?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the governing standard on file with a revision and a date, and does every designer know which one applies to them?
steps.whatToDo: Copy the master checklist and fill the Setup tab first: project details, then the seven module switches. Those switches decide which of the 378 checks apply to this product.
steps.guidelines: Open the DFM/DFT Master Checklist and complete the Setup tab before any layout begins. Record which standard governs — the customer's rule deck, the Elecbits house standard, or a merge — with its revision and date. Where the two disagree, write down which wins and why. A project that starts layout without this has no defensible answer when a fabricator later rejects the board, because nobody can say what the board was supposed to comply with.

steps.step: Fabricator and EMS process capability capture
steps.exitTrigger: Capability sheets received from the named fabricator and EMS and loaded into the Parameters tab of the checklist
steps.entryQuestion: Which fabricator and which EMS will actually build this, and do we have their real process capability rather than their sales sheet?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every DFM number in the checklist trace to a capability the named supplier has confirmed in writing?
steps.template: Fabricator and EMS Process Capability Sheet
steps.whatToDo: Create the sheet and enter the fabricator's and EMS's real limits — track and gap, drill, annular ring, aspect ratio, registration, stencil, placement accuracy, smallest package. Each row needs a written confirmation from the supplier.
steps.guidelines: Ask the fabricator and the EMS for their capability sheet — minimum track and gap, minimum drill, annular ring, aspect ratio, registration tolerance, stencil and paste capability, placement accuracy and the smallest package they run without a quality penalty. Load the real numbers into the Parameters tab. Designing to a generic house default and discovering at fab that the supplier cannot hold it is the single most common cause of a respin at Elecbits.

steps.exitTrigger: Every parameter in the checklist carries an applied value — either the Elecbits default or a recorded customer override with a reason
steps.entryQuestion: Where does the customer's rule differ from ours or from the supplier's capability, and which one wins?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every override recorded with a reason and a source, and has the customer seen the applied set?
steps.whatToDo: Go to the Parameters tab. Leave Customer Override blank where the house default stands; fill it where the customer or the supplier imposes a different number, and name the source. Never edit a number inside a check.
steps.guidelines: Work down the Parameters tab. Leave the Customer Override blank where the house default stands; fill it where the customer or the supplier imposes a different number, and write the source into the Source column. The applied value computes automatically and every rule in the checklist picks it up. Never edit a number inside a check — the whole point is that each number lives in exactly one place and can be defended.

steps.step: DFM/DFT Gate G0 review and sign-off
steps.entryTrigger: Parameter set agreed with the customer and the supplier
steps.exitTrigger: G0 released on the checklist Dashboard — no Critical G0 check left open, failed or unchecked. Layout may begin.
steps.entryQuestion: Do we have everything a designer needs before a single track is routed?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the Dashboard show G0 as RELEASE, and is every exception a recorded waiver with a named approver?
steps.whatToDo: Filter the checklist to G0, answer every active check, then record the gate on the sign-off sheet with all four signatures. Layout does not start on an amber G0.
steps.guidelines: Run the G0 filter on the Master Checklist and answer every active check. G0 is the cheapest gate in the process — everything it catches costs nothing to fix, and everything it misses costs a respin. Do not start layout on an amber G0. If a check cannot be answered because the information does not exist yet, that is a Fail, not a Not-checked.

steps.entryTrigger: Designer LLD locked and trial BOM ordered
steps.exitTrigger: Block diagram drafted with every block, rail and interface shown
steps.entryQuestion: Are all functional blocks, supply rails and interfaces identified in the LLD?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every block in the LLD appear on the diagram with its interfaces and supply named?
steps.whatToDo: Create the HDD and complete the architecture section: every functional block, every supply rail, every interface, and the peripheral map. This is the document the block diagram is drawn from.
steps.guidelines: Draw every functional block with its supply rail, voltage, and the interface between it and its neighbours — a block diagram without rails and interface types is a picture, not a design document. Follow the house drawing rules: font 9, consistent arrow conventions, saved as both editable XML and PNG. This diagram is the shared reference for the firmware and enclosure tracks running in parallel, so it must be readable by people who are not hardware engineers.

steps.step: Block diagram review with checklist - 1st review - self
steps.exitTrigger: Self-review complete with findings corrected
steps.entryQuestion: Has the author walked the diagram against the review checklist before asking for anyone's time?
steps.exitQuestion: Has every checklist item been checked and every finding either fixed or recorded?
steps.whatToDo: Walk every criterion yourself, set Result and Approval, and put your name in Checked by. A criterion left blank is not a pass — it is an unasked question.
steps.guidelines: Walk your own diagram against the checklist before it reaches anyone else — self-review catches the majority of findings at a fraction of the cost of a team review. Check every block against the LLD, every rail against the power budget, every interface for a defined type and direction. Record what you found and fixed; a self-review with no findings usually means it was not done.

steps.step: Block diagram review with checklist - 2nd review
steps.exitTrigger: Second review complete with findings logged and closed
steps.entryQuestion: Is a second reviewer available who did not author the diagram?
steps.exitQuestion: Have all findings been dispositioned — fixed, deferred with rationale, or rejected with reason?
steps.whatToDo: Second reviewer repeats the walk independently. Do not copy the first reviewer's answers; the point of a second pass is that it is a second opinion.
steps.guidelines: A second pair of eyes that did not author the work. Use the same checklist so coverage is comparable across projects and reviewers. Log findings rather than fixing them conversationally — undocumented review findings cannot be audited and the same class of issue recurs on the next board. Each finding gets a disposition: fixed, deferred with rationale, or rejected with reason.

steps.step: Block diagram review with FW & Enclosure team
steps.exitTrigger: Cross-domain review held and interface commitments agreed
steps.entryQuestion: Have firmware and enclosure leads received the diagram in advance?
steps.exitQuestion: Do firmware and enclosure both accept the interfaces and constraints this diagram commits them to?
steps.whatToDo: Add a review record for the cross-team session: interfaces, peripheral map and board outline intent, with every disagreement written down rather than resolved verbally.
steps.responsibility: Hardware Engineer / Firmware Lead / Enclosure Lead
steps.guidelines: This is the first convergence point between the three parallel tracks. Firmware needs the peripheral map, pin allocation and boot strategy; enclosure needs board outline intent, connector positions, thermal sources and mounting. Both must accept what the diagram commits them to. Disagreements found here cost hours; the same disagreements found at prototype cost a board spin.

steps.exitTrigger: Block diagram released as a versioned baseline
steps.entryQuestion: Are all review findings closed and is the version incremented?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the released file stored in the project folder under the naming convention, in both XML and PNG?
steps.whatToDo: Log the block diagram release in the revision index: revision number, date, what changed, and who approved it.
steps.guidelines: Release means frozen and versioned, not merely finished. Store both the editable source and the exported image in the project folder under the naming convention. Downstream tracks now design against this version, so any subsequent change goes through change control with its impact on firmware and enclosure stated — this is precisely the point where a silent edit propagates into two other tracks unnoticed.

steps.exitTrigger: Schematic structure planned and sheet breakdown agreed
steps.entryQuestion: How many boards, sheets and revisions does this architecture require?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every functional block have a designated sheet and does every board have its Eb-PCB ID?
steps.whatToDo: Add the schematic plan to the HDD: how many boards, how many sheets, what sits on each, and which revisions are expected.
steps.guidelines: Decide the board count and the sheet breakdown before drawing anything. One sheet per functional section — power, MCU, interface, sensor, actuator, test points — makes review tractable and PDF export meaningful; a single sprawling sheet cannot be reviewed properly by anyone. Confirm each board carries its Eb-PCB ID. Splitting a board later is a redesign, so make this decision deliberately now.

steps.exitTrigger: Test point strategy documented per net class
steps.entryQuestion: Which nets must remain measurable after assembly, and why?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every net in the board-level functional test parameters have a defined access method?
steps.whatToDo: Open the Net Accessibility tab and start it now, at schematic stage. List every net the board-level functional test must reach, classify it Critical or Standard, and note the intended test point.
steps.guidelines: Work backwards from the board-level functional test parameters: every parameter to be measured needs an accessible net. Classify nets by domain and signal class, decide test point, edge connector or no access, and record the reason plus the alternative method wherever a net is deliberately left inaccessible. Populate the Net Accessibility register as you go — filling it after layout is a documentation exercise, filling it now is a design decision.

steps.entryTrigger: Schematic structure planned and test point strategy set
steps.exitTrigger: Power section drawn with topology, protection and derating applied
steps.entryQuestion: Is the power budget complete, with worst-case load on every rail?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every rail meet its load with margin, and is every part derated against the reliability parameters?
steps.whatToDo: Record the power section decisions in the HDD: topology, worst-case power budget, protection scheme and the derating applied to each part.
steps.guidelines: Draw the power tree from input protection through each regulation stage to every rail, sized against worst-case simultaneous load rather than typical. Apply the derating rules from the reliability parameters — voltage, current and temperature margin on every part. Where the design touches mains, creepage and clearance follow the certification route decided at feasibility and are not engineering defaults to be assumed. Show sequencing and any supervisory or reset circuitry explicitly.

steps.exitTrigger: MCU section drawn with pin allocation, boot, debug and reset complete
steps.entryQuestion: Is the MCU selection confirmed with I/O margin against the LLD?
steps.exitQuestion: Has firmware confirmed the pin map, boot strategy and debug interface?
steps.whatToDo: Record the MCU section: part choice with its justification, the full pin map, boot and reset strategy, and the debug interface.
steps.guidelines: Draw the MCU with its decoupling, crystal or oscillator, reset, boot-mode strapping and debug header. Allocate pins against the LLD's I/O count with its 20–30% margin held in reserve — margin consumed during schematic capture is not margin. Share the pin map with firmware before it is final; a pin allocation that firmware cannot use is discovered at bring-up, and by then it is a board spin.

steps.exitTrigger: Interface section drawn with protection and level translation complete
steps.entryQuestion: Is every external interface specified with its connector, protection and signalling level?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every externally exposed pin carry ESD protection appropriate to the environment?
steps.whatToDo: Record the interface section: each connector, its pinout, its protection and the mating half it expects.
steps.guidelines: Draw every external interface with its connector, ESD protection, level translation and termination. Every pin that leaves the enclosure is an ESD path and needs protection sized to the environmental parameters. Confirm connector part numbers and their mechanical footprints with the enclosure track — connector choice is a mechanical decision as much as an electrical one and it is the commonest cause of first-article fit failure.

steps.exitTrigger: Sensor section drawn with conditioning, filtering and reference design applied
steps.entryQuestion: Is each sensor's accuracy, range and conditioning requirement defined?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the analog front end meet the accuracy stated in the electrical test parameters?
steps.whatToDo: Record the sensor section: each sensor, its accuracy target, its conditioning, and how it will be calibrated.
steps.guidelines: Draw each sensor with its conditioning: gain, filtering, reference and ADC path. Check the noise and accuracy budget against the electrical test parameters rather than assuming the sensor datasheet figure survives the front end — it usually does not. Follow the manufacturer's reference layout guidance where one exists, and note any grounding or partition requirement now so it survives into layout.

steps.exitTrigger: Actuator section drawn with drive, protection and flyback handling complete
steps.entryQuestion: What is the worst-case load, inrush and fault condition on each output?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every inductive load clamped and is every output protected against short and overload?
steps.whatToDo: Record the actuator and output section: drive topology, worst-case load, protection and thermal assumption.
steps.guidelines: Size drive circuitry against worst-case load including inrush, not steady-state. Clamp every inductive load; an unclamped relay or motor will destroy its driver and the failure appears intermittently in the field. Provide short-circuit and overload protection on outputs that reach the outside world. Check thermal dissipation in the switching devices against the thermal budget at maximum duty.

steps.exitTrigger: Test points and debug headers added to schematic
steps.entryQuestion: Does the test point strategy translate to actual placed test points on every required net?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every net named in the Net Accessibility register present, or its inaccessibility justified?
steps.whatToDo: Update the Net Accessibility tab with the test points and debug headers actually placed on the schematic, and mark which nets still have no access.
steps.guidelines: Add the test points the strategy calls for, plus programming and debug headers. Reconcile against the Net Accessibility register net by net and record the reason and alternative method for every net deliberately left inaccessible. Test points added at this stage cost nothing; test points discovered missing during bring-up cost a spin, and this is the single most common cause of production test coverage gaps.

steps.step: Schematic review with checklist - 1st review - self
steps.exitTrigger: Self-review complete with findings corrected
steps.entryQuestion: Has the author walked the full checklist section by section?
steps.exitQuestion: Have all ERC warnings been resolved or explicitly justified?
steps.whatToDo: Walk every criterion against the drawn schematic, not against your intent. Set Result, Approval and Checked by on every row.
steps.guidelines: Run the electrical rule check and resolve every warning — a suppressed ERC warning is a deferred failure. Walk the checklist section by section: rails, decoupling, pull-ups and pull-downs, unconnected pins, reference designators, part values, footprint assignments. Check every net name for typos, because a mistyped net name creates a silent disconnection that survives every visual review.

steps.exitTrigger: Peer or lead review complete with findings logged and closed
steps.entryQuestion: Is the reviewer someone who did not author the schematic and has read the LLD?
steps.exitQuestion: Has every finding been dispositioned and re-verified after correction?
steps.whatToDo: Independent second review. The reviewer must be someone who did not draw the sheets.
steps.guidelines: Independent review against the same checklist. The reviewer reads the LLD first — a schematic review without the requirement document checks internal consistency but not correctness. Log every finding with a disposition and re-verify after correction; findings closed without re-check are the ones that reach the board. Arun is the technical authority for hardware where a finding is disputed.

steps.step: BoM components verification - Obsolescence and Cost
steps.exitTrigger: BOM verified for lifecycle and costed against target
steps.entryQuestion: Is every part's lifecycle status and current price checked against a live distributor source?
steps.exitQuestion: Is any part NRND or obsolete, and does the BOM land within the target COGS?
steps.whatToDo: Create the verification sheet and check every BOM line for lifecycle status, last-time-buy date, stock, lead time and unit cost at production volume.
steps.guidelines: Check every line for lifecycle status and current pricing against live distributor data, not a cached BOM from a previous project. Flag anything NRND, last-time-buy or with lead time beyond the build schedule, and identify alternates for each. Total the BOM against the target COGS agreed at feasibility — a BOM discovered over target after layout leaves only expensive options. Begin vendor RFQ now rather than waiting for the commercials stage.

steps.exitTrigger: BOM verified for compliance with certificates collected
steps.entryQuestion: Does every part carry the certifications the target market and standard require?
steps.exitQuestion: Are RoHS, REACH and any safety-critical part approvals on file for every applicable line?
steps.whatToDo: Add the compliance columns: RoHS, REACH and any market-specific restriction, each evidenced by a supplier declaration for the exact part number bought.
steps.guidelines: Collect RoHS and REACH declarations for every line and safety agency approvals for every safety-critical part — fuses, Y-capacitors, optocouplers, transformers, mains connectors. A safety-critical part without the right approval marking fails certification regardless of how well the circuit performs, and substituting it late invalidates the safety testing already done. File the certificates against the project now, while the supplier is responsive.

steps.step: Schematic review with FW & Enclosure team
steps.exitTrigger: Cross-domain schematic review held and commitments confirmed
steps.entryQuestion: Have firmware and enclosure received the schematic PDF and BOM in advance?
steps.exitQuestion: Do firmware and enclosure both accept the pin map, connectors and mechanical constraints?
steps.whatToDo: Add the cross-team schematic review: pin map agreed with firmware, connectors and mechanical constraints agreed with enclosure.
steps.responsibility: Hardware Engineer / Firmware Lead / Enclosure Lead
steps.guidelines: Second convergence point across the three tracks. Firmware confirms the pin map, peripheral assignment, boot strategy and debug access are usable. Enclosure confirms connector part numbers, their orientations, indicator positions and thermal sources. Both sign what they are accepting. After this review the schematic goes to release and changes become expensive in two other tracks, not just this one.

steps.entryTrigger: New parts identified during schematic capture
steps.exitTrigger: All new components registered with verified symbol, footprint and 3D model
steps.entryQuestion: Which parts on this BOM do not already exist in the Component Libraries?
steps.exitQuestion: Has each new footprint been dimensionally verified against the datasheet by a second person?
steps.whatToDo: Add each new component to the selection criteria register with the reason it was chosen over the alternatives, and its second source.
steps.guidelines: Register every new part in the Component Libraries with symbol, verified footprint, 3D model, lifecycle status and approved sources. This is enforced, not optional — an unregistered part is invisible to the next project and the same verification work is repeated. Have a second person check the footprint against the datasheet dimensionally; an unverified footprint is the most expensive single error in PCB design because it is only discovered at assembly.

steps.exitTrigger: Analog simulation complete with results documented
steps.entryQuestion: Which analog circuits carry enough risk to justify simulation?
steps.exitQuestion: Do simulated results meet the electrical test parameters at worst-case corners?
steps.whatToDo: Record the analogue simulation: what was simulated, the model assumptions, the result, and what it changed in the design.
steps.guidelines: Simulate the circuits where being wrong is expensive: power stages, feedback loops, analog front ends, protection networks. Run worst-case corners for tolerance, temperature and load rather than nominal only — nominal-only simulation confirms the design works in conditions it will never see. Compare results against the electrical test parameters and store the simulation files with the project so the result can be reproduced.

steps.exitTrigger: Digital simulation complete with termination and timing verified
steps.entryQuestion: Which digital interfaces run fast enough or far enough to need pre-layout analysis?
steps.exitQuestion: Are termination strategy and timing margin defined before layout constrains them?
steps.whatToDo: Record the digital simulation the same way, including the cases that failed and what was done about them.
steps.guidelines: Analyse the interfaces where edge rate or trace length matters — high-speed serial, memory buses, clock distribution. The output is a termination strategy, a topology and a length-matching requirement that layout must honour. Doing this after layout produces a report about a board that is already wrong; doing it now produces constraints that make the layout right the first time.

steps.entryTrigger: All reviews closed and simulations complete
steps.exitTrigger: Schematic released as a versioned, dated baseline with PDF export
steps.entryQuestion: Are all findings closed, ERC clean, and the version incremented?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the released PDF stored in the project folder under the naming convention?
steps.whatToDo: Log the schematic release: revision, date, changes since the last revision, and the approver.
steps.guidelines: Release the schematic as a frozen, versioned, dated baseline with a PDF export organised by section. This is the reference every downstream artefact is built from — layout, BOM, test, assembly documentation. Store under the naming convention in the project folder. Post-release changes go through change control with their impact on firmware, enclosure and BOM stated explicitly.

steps.exitTrigger: Project archive released with libraries and design rules included
steps.entryQuestion: Are all project source files, libraries and settings consistent and archived?
steps.exitQuestion: Could another engineer open this archive on a clean machine and rebuild the design?
steps.whatToDo: Log the project file release and record where the source files live and at what tag.
steps.guidelines: Archive the complete project: schematic source, PCB source, project file, integrated libraries and design rule set. Test the archive by opening it somewhere without your local library paths — a project that only builds on the author's machine is not archived, and this is discovered at the worst possible moment, usually when that person has left or is unavailable. Store under the project ID.

steps.step: Final Bill of Materials (BOM) - Electronics release
steps.exitTrigger: Electronics BOM released with alternates and sources
steps.entryQuestion: Are all designators, quantities, part numbers and alternates final?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every line have a manufacturer part number, at least one approved source, and an alternate where lead time is long?
steps.whatToDo: Freeze the electronics BOM at this revision. Record the revision number — every later document that cites a BOM must cite this one.
steps.guidelines: Release the BOM with manufacturer part numbers, designators, quantities, approved sources and alternates. Every line needs a real manufacturer part number — a description without a part number will be substituted by a vendor exercising their own judgement. Mark the safety-critical parts explicitly, because those cannot be substituted at all without re-running the safety assessment. Hand to procurement for RFQ against the target COGS.

steps.entryTrigger: BOM released and layer count estimated
steps.exitTrigger: Candidate stackups identified from the fabricator's standard set
steps.entryQuestion: Which stackups has this fabricator already proven, and what are their tolerances?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the selected stackup one the fabricator builds routinely, or a special order?
steps.whatToDo: Read the stack-up reference and pick a candidate stack that the fabricator already runs. Do not invent a stack-up.
steps.guidelines: Start from the fabricator's standard, proven stackups rather than designing one from first principles — a non-standard stackup costs more, takes longer and carries more impedance variation. Note the dielectric constants, copper weights and tolerances they actually hold, because impedance calculations built on generic values do not survive contact with a real fabricator.

steps.exitTrigger: Stackup finalised and impedance targets confirmed with the fabricator
steps.entryQuestion: Does the stackup support the impedance, current and layer count the design requires?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the fabricator confirmed they can hold the stated impedance on this stackup?
steps.whatToDo: Create the stack-up definition: layer count, copper weights, dielectric materials and thicknesses, and the impedance targets confirmed by the fabricator.
steps.guidelines: Fix layer count, dielectric thicknesses, copper weights and impedance targets, then have the fabricator confirm in writing that they can hold them. Copper weight follows the current requirement from the power design; layer count follows routing density and the need for continuous reference planes under high-speed signals. Record the stackup in the project folder — it is an input to fabrication, impedance control and DFM review alike.

steps.exitTrigger: DRC rule set configured and saved to the project
steps.entryQuestion: Are the fabricator's capability limits and the design's electrical constraints both captured as rules?
steps.exitQuestion: Do the rules encode creepage and clearance for the certification route, not just fabrication minimums?
steps.whatToDo: Build the CAD DRC rule set from the applied values on the Parameters tab. The rules and the checklist must carry the same numbers, or one of them is lying.
steps.guidelines: Configure rules from two sources: the fabricator's capability limits for track, gap, drill and annular ring, and the design's own constraints for impedance, length matching and creepage. Where mains or high voltage is present, encode the creepage and clearance from the actual certification route — these are the parameters most often left at engineering defaults and they are the ones that fail certification. Save the rule file into the project so it travels with the design.

steps.exitTrigger: Board outline and keep-outs defined from the enclosure CAD
steps.entryQuestion: Has the enclosure track provided the outline, mounting positions and internal keep-outs?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the outline derive from the enclosure model rather than being estimated?
steps.whatToDo: Record the board outline and keep-outs in the HDD, referencing the enclosure CAD revision they were taken from.
steps.guidelines: Take the outline from the enclosure CAD, not from an estimate — enclosure dimensions are finalised before schematic and layout precisely so this transfer is possible. Define mounting holes, connector cut-out positions, component height limits per zone, and keep-outs for bosses, ribs and internal features. An outline guessed at this step produces a board that does not fit, discovered at first article.

steps.step: Board Outline review with Enclosure team
steps.exitTrigger: Outline confirmed against the enclosure model and both sides agree the revision
steps.entryQuestion: Does the enclosure team agree the outline matches their current CAD revision?
steps.exitQuestion: Are both tracks working from the same CAD revision number?
steps.whatToDo: Add the outline review with enclosure: outline, mounting, keep-outs and connector positions, checked against a named CAD revision.
steps.guidelines: Confirm the outline against the enclosure model with both revision numbers stated out loud. The failure mode here is not disagreement but drift — each track working from a different revision of the same model, each internally consistent, discovered at fit check. Agree explicitly how a future enclosure change will be notified to hardware and vice versa.

steps.exitTrigger: Placement plan documented and critical placement complete
steps.entryQuestion: Is the placement strategy decided before any component is placed?
steps.exitQuestion: Are power, analog, digital and RF partitioned, and are thermal sources placed against the thermal plan?
steps.whatToDo: Write the layout plan into Design Notes before routing: placement strategy, critical nets, return paths, thermal plan and what must not move.
steps.guidelines: Plan before placing. Partition the board into power, analog, digital and RF domains and keep return paths within their domains. Place the fixed items first — connectors, mounting holes, indicators, antenna — because these are mechanically constrained and everything else moves around them. Place thermal sources against the thermal budget and give them copper. Placement determines routing quality more than routing skill does; time spent here is recovered several times over.

steps.exitTrigger: Power and high-current nets routed and verified
steps.entryQuestion: Are trace widths calculated against actual current and permitted temperature rise?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every power trace meet its IPC-2221 width for the current and copper weight?
steps.whatToDo: Answer the G1 checks in section 6 (pattern and routing) and section 22 (thermal and derating) as you route the power nets. Trace widths come from a calculation, not a habit.
steps.guidelines: Route power first, while the space to do it properly still exists. Calculate widths per IPC-2221 against actual current and permitted temperature rise rather than by eye. Use planes or polygons for high current, keep loops tight, and place bulk and decoupling capacitance so the high-frequency return path is short. Where mains is present, the creepage and clearance from the certification route apply here physically and are checked in DFM review.

steps.exitTrigger: High-speed nets routed to their constraints and verified
steps.entryQuestion: Are the length matching, impedance and topology constraints from digital simulation loaded?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every high-speed net have a continuous reference plane beneath it for its full length?
steps.whatToDo: Answer the section 6 checks for high-speed nets: impedance, reference continuity, length matching and via transitions.
steps.guidelines: Route high-speed signals against the constraints produced by digital simulation: impedance, length match, topology and termination placement. Every high-speed net needs a continuous reference plane for its whole length — a net crossing a plane split has no defined return path and produces emissions that fail radiated compliance and are extremely hard to diagnose after the fact. Minimise layer changes; add stitching vias where they are unavoidable.

steps.exitTrigger: All remaining nets routed and connectivity verified
steps.entryQuestion: Are the remaining nets routed without compromising the power and high-speed work already done?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the board fully routed with zero unrouted nets and no rule violations introduced?
steps.whatToDo: Answer the remaining section 6 checks for general signals, including clearance to board edge and to the mains domain if one exists.
steps.guidelines: Route what remains without cutting planes or crossing splits that the earlier passes depended on. Keep sensitive analog away from switching nodes and clocks. Check connectivity completeness — an unrouted net at this stage is easy to miss visually and is caught only by the rule check, which is why the clean DRC step exists and must not be skipped.

steps.exitTrigger: Pours and planes complete with stitching applied
steps.entryQuestion: Are plane splits deliberate, and does every split respect the return paths of the signals crossing it?
steps.exitQuestion: Are there any isolated copper islands, unconnected thermal pads or orphaned pours?
steps.whatToDo: Answer the section 3 and section 6 checks for planes: split integrity, return path continuity and thermal relief on every plane connection.
steps.guidelines: Pour planes with deliberate splits that follow the domain partitioning, and check that no signal crosses a split without a return path. Add stitching vias at layer transitions and around the board edge. Look specifically for isolated copper islands and orphaned pours — these are antennas in the emissions test and they are invisible on a casual visual inspection.

steps.exitTrigger: Silkscreen complete with polarity, pin 1 and safety markings placed
steps.entryQuestion: Is every designator readable, correctly oriented and not obscured by its own component?
steps.exitQuestion: Are polarity and pin 1 indicators visible after the component is fitted?
steps.whatToDo: Answer the section 8 checks: every designator visible after assembly, polarity marks present, no silkscreen over a pad or a test point.
steps.guidelines: Place designators so they remain readable with components fitted, and keep silkscreen off pads. Mark polarity, pin 1, connector orientation and any high-voltage warning. Include the board name, Eb-PCB ID, revision and date. Silkscreen is the assembly line's only in-situ documentation — a board that cannot be assembled correctly from its own markings will be assembled incorrectly at least once.

steps.exitTrigger: DRC and connectivity checks pass with zero unresolved violations
steps.entryQuestion: Have all design rules been re-verified against the final fabricator capability set?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every remaining waiver documented with its rationale and approver?
steps.whatToDo: Record the DRC run in Design Notes: rule set version, error count, and every waived violation with the reason it was waived.
steps.guidelines: Run the full rule check and connectivity check and drive them to zero. Where a violation is genuinely acceptable, waive it explicitly with rationale and approver recorded — an undocumented waiver is indistinguishable from an oversight when the board fails. Re-run after every subsequent edit, however small; a late change that reintroduces a violation is the classic route to a failed fabrication.

steps.entryTrigger: Placement complete and a clean DRC achieved
steps.exitTrigger: Every net classified on the Net Accessibility register with a measured coverage figure computed
steps.entryQuestion: Which nets must the production test actually reach, and has anyone counted them since placement moved?
steps.exitQuestion: What is the coverage figure, and is it at or above what the board-level functional test parameters assumed?
steps.whatToDo: Export the netlist into the Net Accessibility tab and classify every net. The coverage figure computes at the top of the tab — it is a number, not an impression.
steps.guidelines: Export the netlist and walk it into the Net Accessibility tab. Mark each net Critical, Standard or Ignore, give it a signal class, and record whether a test point exists. The test point strategy was set at schematic time, before placement and routing moved everything — this is the step that checks whether the strategy survived the layout. Coverage is a number, not an impression, and it belongs in the file.

steps.step: DFT — probe access and fixture feasibility review
steps.exitTrigger: Probe pitch, keep-outs, tooling holes and board support verified against the fixture house's stated rules
steps.entryQuestion: Can a bed-of-nails or flying-probe fixture actually land on this board as drawn?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the fixture house or the production engineer confirmed in writing that the board is fixturable?
steps.whatToDo: Answer sections 10, 11 and 12 — test point provision, geometry and four-wire measurement — against the real layout, then get the fixture house to confirm the board is fixturable.
steps.guidelines: Check probe pitch against the minimum the fixture house can hold, confirm tooling holes exist and are not obstructed, and verify the board can be supported without pressing on tall or fragile components. Send the layout to whoever will build the fixture and get a written confirmation. Discovering at Mass Production that the fixture cannot be built is a change to a frozen design — the most expensive change there is.

steps.step: DFT — programming, boundary scan and debug access review
steps.exitTrigger: Programming contacts, boot-mode control and the diagnostic interface confirmed reachable from one board side without a jumper
steps.entryQuestion: Can the line program and interrogate this board without a human opening it or moving a link?
steps.exitQuestion: Are programming and test access on the same board side, and does the programming cycle fit the time budget?
steps.template: Firmware Test Hooks and Diagnostic Command Set
steps.whatToDo: Create the command set sheet and record the programming interface: contacts, board side, reset and boot-mode control, and whether the fixture can drive all of it without a jumper.
steps.guidelines: Confirm the programming interface is exposed as pogo-compatible pads with at least the parameter contact count, that reset and boot-mode can be driven by the fixture, and that no jumper or human step sits inside the cycle. A two-sided fixture doubles the cost and halves the throughput; a jumper inside the cycle means the line will skip it. Verify the diagnostic interface baud is fixed rather than auto-detected.

steps.exitTrigger: Every inaccessible net carries either a new test point or a written alternative test method, and the count with neither is zero
steps.entryQuestion: For each net we cannot reach, how else will we know it is good before the unit ships?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the count of inaccessible nets with no alternative method zero on the register?
steps.whatToDo: For every net marked inaccessible, fill either a new test point reference or a written alternative test method. The count with neither must reach zero before you leave this step.
steps.guidelines: For every net marked inaccessible, either add a test point now — while the layout is still open — or write down how it will be tested instead: a functional route, a firmware readback, a boundary-scan chain, or an accepted risk. An inaccessible net with a blank alternative is an untested net that will be found in the field. This is the last moment adding a test point is free.

steps.exitTrigger: DFM review complete with findings addressed
steps.entryQuestion: Has the design been checked against the fabricator's actual process capability?
steps.exitQuestion: Are annular rings, drill sizes, solder mask slivers and panel edge clearances all within capability?
steps.whatToDo: Answer the G1 fabrication checks — sections 3 to 8 — against the fabricator's confirmed capability rather than a generic rule.
steps.guidelines: Check the design against what the fabricator can actually build: minimum annular ring, drill-to-copper, solder mask sliver and dam widths, acid traps, panel edge clearance. Run the DFM tooling where available. Findings here are cheap; the same findings raised by the fabricator after file submission cost a week of back-and-forth and often a compromise made under time pressure.

steps.exitTrigger: DFA review complete with assembly findings addressed
steps.entryQuestion: Can this board actually be assembled at volume by the intended process?
steps.exitQuestion: Are component spacings, orientations and fiducials adequate for automated placement and inspection?
steps.whatToDo: Answer section 9, assembly process and poka-yoke: spacing, orientation, polarity, wave-solder clearance and anything that lets the line build it wrong.
steps.guidelines: Check assembly feasibility: component-to-component spacing for placement and rework, consistent orientation to reduce placement error, fiducials for machine vision, adequate clearance for AOI and for test probes. Check that no component blocks access to another or to a test point. Assembly problems found here are layout edits; found at the EMS they are line stoppages and unit-cost increases.

steps.step: DFx review with Checklist - 1st review - self
steps.exitTrigger: Self DFx review complete with findings corrected
steps.entryQuestion: Has the author walked the full DFx checklist personally?
steps.exitQuestion: Has every applicable checklist item been assessed and recorded, not just the ones that seemed relevant?
steps.whatToDo: The author walks the full G1 filter personally and corrects what fails. Findings go back into the layout at this step, not onto a list for later.
steps.guidelines: Walk the DFM/DFT checklist personally before the formal review. Assess every applicable item and record the result — the value of a 300-item checklist is entirely in the items nobody would have thought to check. Record measured values where the check has a parameter rather than marking it pass; an unmeasured pass on a safety spacing parameter is not a check, and these parameters are the ones that fail certification.

steps.exitTrigger: Formal DFx review complete, findings dispositioned, waivers registered
steps.entryQuestion: Is the reviewer independent, and is the certification route confirmed so the safety parameters can be checked correctly?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every safety-derived finding either closed or carried in the waiver register with customer approval?
steps.whatToDo: Independent reviewer repeats the G1 walk. Every finding is dispositioned — fixed, or raised as a waiver.
steps.guidelines: Independent review against the checklist with owner and target date assigned to every open finding. Confirm the certification route first, because the safety spacing parameters follow from it and cannot be assessed against engineering defaults. Any finding that cannot be closed goes into the waiver register with its safety-derived flag set — a safety-derived rule cannot be waived by Elecbits alone and needs the customer approver named.

steps.step: DFM/DFT Gate G1 review and sign-off
steps.entryTrigger: DFM considerations, DFA considerations and both DFx checklist reviews complete with findings corrected
steps.exitTrigger: G1 released on the Dashboard — no Critical G1 check left open, failed or unchecked
steps.entryQuestion: Has every G1 check been answered against the actual layout rather than the design intent?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the Dashboard show G1 as RELEASE, and is every finding either fixed in the layout or waived?
steps.whatToDo: Confirm the Dashboard shows G1 as RELEASE, then record the gate on the sign-off sheet against the exact file revision reviewed.
steps.guidelines: G1 is the bulk of the checklist and the reason the file exists. Answer it against the board that is actually drawn — open the layout alongside the checklist and measure. A check answered from memory is a check not run. Findings go back into the layout before G1 is signed, not onto a to-do list for later.

steps.exitTrigger: STEP file reviewed and verified against the layout
steps.entryQuestion: Does the STEP export include all components with correct heights and positions?
steps.exitQuestion: Are all tall components, connectors and mounting features represented at their true height?
steps.whatToDo: Add the STEP file review: component heights, positions, and the tall parts checked against the enclosure at worst-case tolerance.
steps.guidelines: Export the STEP with all component 3D bodies and check it against the layout. Verify tall components, connectors and anything near the enclosure wall at true height — a missing or default-height 3D body is the usual cause of a fit failure that nobody predicted. This file is the enclosure track's only accurate view of the board, so its correctness matters to a track you cannot see.

steps.step: PCB STEP File review with enclosure team
steps.exitTrigger: Joint fit review complete with clearances confirmed
steps.entryQuestion: Has the enclosure team imported the STEP into the current CAD assembly?
steps.exitQuestion: Are there any interferences, and is there adequate clearance for assembly access and tolerance?
steps.whatToDo: Add the joint STEP review with enclosure: interference and clearance at the tolerance extremes, not at nominal.
steps.guidelines: Import into the enclosure assembly and check for interference and clearance together, in one session. Check assembly access as well as static fit — a board that fits but cannot be inserted past a boss is still a failure. Confirm connector alignment with their apertures and check clearance against the tolerance stack-up rather than against nominal dimensions.

steps.exitTrigger: Signal, power and thermal simulation complete with results documented
steps.entryQuestion: Which nets or thermal paths carry enough risk to justify post-layout simulation?
steps.exitQuestion: Do post-layout results still meet the constraints assumed during schematic simulation?
steps.whatToDo: Create the PI/SI report and record the simulation setup, the results, and the margin against each target.
steps.guidelines: Run post-layout signal integrity, power integrity and thermal analysis on the paths that carry risk. This verifies the actual routed geometry rather than the intended topology, and the two diverge more often than expected. Compare against the pre-layout assumptions and against the thermal budget. Document the results; where a marginal result is accepted, record why and what will be measured on the first article to confirm it.

steps.entryTrigger: Joint fit review closed and simulation complete
steps.exitTrigger: STEP file released as a versioned baseline to the enclosure track
steps.entryQuestion: Are all fit findings closed and the layout final?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the released STEP match the layout revision going to fabrication?
steps.whatToDo: Log the STEP file release with its revision and the CAD version it was exported from.
steps.guidelines: Release the STEP at the same revision as the layout going to fabrication and state that revision when handing it over. The enclosure track will finalise CAD against this file, so a mismatch between released STEP and fabricated board produces an enclosure that fits a board that was never built. Store under the naming convention.

steps.entryTrigger: Layout final and all reviews closed
steps.exitTrigger: Gerber, Excellon and IPC-356 files released to fabrication
steps.entryQuestion: Have the Gerbers been re-imported and visually verified layer by layer?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the netlist test file match the design netlist exactly?
steps.whatToDo: Log the Gerber release. Record every file in the pack and its revision — this is what the fabricator will actually build.
steps.guidelines: Generate Gerber, Excellon drill and IPC-356 netlist, then re-import them into a viewer and check layer by layer against the layout — export settings drift and a wrong aperture or missing layer is only visible on re-import. The IPC-356 netlist lets the fabricator electrically test the bare board against the intended design and should always be included. Release under the Eb-PCB ID with its revision.

steps.exitTrigger: Panel design reviewed with fabricator and EMS
steps.entryQuestion: Does the panel layout match the assembly line's handling and depaneling requirements?
steps.exitQuestion: Are rail widths, fiducials, tooling holes and depaneling method agreed by the assembler?
steps.whatToDo: Answer section 3, board and panel: array size against the EMS machine envelope, spacing between sub-boards, guide holes and fiducials.
steps.guidelines: Review the panel with both the fabricator and the assembler, since it must satisfy both. Check rail width for conveyor handling, global fiducials, tooling holes, board spacing and the depaneling method — V-score or tab-route — against the board edge components. Depaneling stress is a real cause of ceramic capacitor cracking near board edges, and it is designed out here or not at all.

steps.exitTrigger: Panel Gerbers released to fabrication
steps.entryQuestion: Have all panel findings been incorporated and re-verified?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the released panel file at the same revision as the released board Gerbers?
steps.whatToDo: Log the panel Gerber release with the panel drawing revision.
steps.guidelines: Release the panel files at the board revision they correspond to, and state the correspondence. A panel file released against a superseded board revision produces a full panel of wrong boards, and the error is not visible until first article. Store with the board Gerbers under the same Eb-PCB ID and revision.
