steps.exitTrigger: Pick and place file reviewed against the layout and the assembler's format
steps.entryQuestion: Are the origin, units, rotation convention and side designation correct for the assembler?
steps.exitQuestion: Do the rotations match the assembler's convention rather than the EDA tool's default?
steps.whatToDo: Check the pick-and-place file: every placed part present, correct rotation convention, correct origin, and the units stated.
steps.guidelines: Check origin, units, rotation convention and top/bottom designation against what the assembler actually consumes. Rotation convention is the recurring failure: EDA defaults and assembler expectations differ, and a systematic rotation error places every polarised part backwards across the whole build. Confirm the convention in writing with the EMS before release rather than assuming the industry standard applies.

steps.exitTrigger: Pick and place file released to the assembler
steps.entryQuestion: Is the file at the same revision as the released Gerbers and BOM?
steps.exitQuestion: Do designators in this file reconcile exactly with the BOM and the assembly drawing?
steps.whatToDo: Release the pick-and-place file and log the revision it matches on the BOM and the Gerbers.
steps.guidelines: Release with the Gerbers and BOM at matching revisions, and reconcile designators across all three — a designator present in one and absent in another stops the line while someone works out which is right. Store under the Eb-PCB ID and revision.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly drawing reviewed for completeness and clarity
steps.entryQuestion: Does the drawing show everything an assembler needs that the pick and place file does not carry?
steps.exitQuestion: Are polarity, orientation, do-not-populate and special-process items all called out?
steps.whatToDo: Check the assembly line document against the layout: correct revision, correct orientation marks, and every special instruction the line needs.
steps.guidelines: Check that the drawing shows both sides, all designators, polarity and orientation markings, do-not-populate items, and any special process such as hand-soldered, heatsinked or torqued parts. Do-not-populate is the most commonly missed call-out and produces a build that is electrically wrong in a way that passes visual inspection. The drawing must be readable when printed at A3.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly drawing released as PDF to the assembler
steps.entryQuestion: Is the drawing at the same revision as the Gerbers, BOM and pick and place file?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the drawing revision consistent with the rest of the fabrication package?
steps.whatToDo: Release the assembly line document and record which build it is for.
steps.guidelines: Release as PDF at the matching revision and include it in the fabrication package. Every document in that package carries the same Eb-PCB ID and revision so the assembler can verify at a glance that they hold one consistent set rather than a mixture from two design iterations.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly instruction reviewed against the actual assembly process
steps.entryQuestion: Does the instruction cover sequence, process parameters and inspection criteria?
steps.exitQuestion: Are the reflow profile, hand-solder steps and inspection criteria all specified?
steps.whatToDo: Check the assembly instruction document: can someone who has never seen this board build it correctly from this alone?
steps.guidelines: Review the sequence: solder paste, placement, reflow profile, hand-soldered items, wash, conformal coat, inspection. Specify the reflow profile against the most thermally sensitive part on the BOM rather than a generic profile. State inspection criteria explicitly — AOI coverage, X-ray for BGAs, what constitutes a reject — because criteria left to the assembler's judgement vary between operators and between shifts.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly instruction released to the EMS
steps.entryQuestion: Has the assembler confirmed they can execute this instruction as written?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the EMS raised any process step they cannot perform or would perform differently?
steps.whatToDo: Release the assembly instruction document at a named revision.
steps.guidelines: Release to the EMS and ask them to confirm they can execute it as written. An EMS that silently substitutes their standard process for a specified one produces units that do not match the qualified build, and this is discovered at reliability testing if at all. Capture any deviation they need as a documented agreement rather than an informal accommodation.

steps.exitTrigger: Wiring document reviewed for completeness
steps.entryQuestion: Are all inter-board and off-board connections specified with connector, pinout and wire spec?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every wire have a gauge, colour, length and termination specified?
steps.whatToDo: Check the wiring document against the assembly drawing and the mechanical BOM: every harness component present, every connection unambiguous.
steps.guidelines: Specify every harness and inter-board connection with connector part numbers, pinouts, wire gauge, colour code, length and termination method. Wire colour coding is not cosmetic — it is what prevents a reversed connection during assembly and what makes field service possible. Check current-carrying capacity and voltage rating on every conductor against the electrical design.

steps.exitTrigger: Wiring document released
steps.entryQuestion: Is the document consistent with the assembly drawing and the mechanical BOM?
steps.exitQuestion: Are all harness components present on the multilevel BOM?
steps.whatToDo: Release the wiring document with wire gauge, colour, length and crimp specification complete.
steps.guidelines: Release and reconcile against the mechanical BOM — harness components are the most commonly omitted BOM lines and their absence is discovered when the build stops for want of a connector housing. Confirm consistency with the assembly drawing so the two documents cannot contradict each other on the line.

steps.entryTrigger: Assembly documentation complete and coating requirement confirmed
steps.exitTrigger: Coating keep-out areas and process reviewed
steps.entryQuestion: Is conformal coating actually required by the environmental parameters?
steps.exitQuestion: Are connectors, test points and heat-dissipating surfaces all masked?
steps.whatToDo: Answer section 14, conformal coating: is coating actually required by the environment, and are the keep-out areas defined on every connector, test point and sensor?
steps.guidelines: Confirm coating is required by the environmental parameters before specifying it — coating adds cost, cycle time and rework difficulty and is sometimes specified by habit. Where it is required, define keep-out areas precisely: connectors, test points, programming headers, thermal interfaces and any adjustable component. Specify the material, thickness and cure. Coated test points cannot be probed, which silently removes production test coverage.

steps.exitTrigger: Coating files and keep-out drawing released
steps.entryQuestion: Are the masking requirements unambiguous to the operator applying them?
steps.exitQuestion: Can an operator identify every masked area from the drawing alone?
steps.whatToDo: Log the conformal coating file release with the coating material and process named.
steps.guidelines: Release the coating drawing with masking areas clearly marked and dimensioned. The operator applying the mask works from this drawing alone, so ambiguity here becomes inconsistent coating across the batch. Include the material specification and cure schedule.

steps.entryTrigger: Design complete and characterisation data available
steps.exitTrigger: Datasheet reviewed for technical accuracy
steps.entryQuestion: Does every specification in the datasheet trace to a measured or simulated result?
steps.exitQuestion: Is any figure in this document a design intent rather than a verified measurement?
steps.whatToDo: Check the datasheet against the design as built: every stated figure traceable to a measurement or a calculation, not to an intention.
steps.guidelines: Check every figure against measured or simulated evidence. A datasheet is a commitment to the client and to their customers, and any number in it that is aspiration rather than measurement will be tested by someone eventually. Mark preliminary figures as preliminary. Include absolute maximum ratings, recommended operating conditions, electrical characteristics with conditions, mechanical dimensions and environmental limits.

steps.exitTrigger: Datasheet released as a versioned document
steps.entryQuestion: Are all specifications final and consistent with the test reports?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the datasheet reconcile with the test reports and the compliance certificates?
steps.whatToDo: Release the product datasheet. Anything externally visible needs client approval before this.
steps.guidelines: Release under version control and reconcile against the test reports and certificates — a datasheet claiming a rating the test report does not support is a liability. Store in the project folder and provide to the client as part of the documentation handover. Update it when design changes affect specifications rather than leaving the released version to drift out of truth.

steps.entryTrigger: Electronics, mechanical and packaging BOMs complete
steps.exitTrigger: Multilevel BOM released covering PCBA, mechanical, harness and packaging
steps.entryQuestion: Is every part of the finished goods item represented at the correct level?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the multilevel BOM total reconcile with the costed budget?
steps.whatToDo: Release the multilevel BOM for ordering: electronics, mechanical and packaging consolidated into one orderable list with quantities per unit.
steps.guidelines: Assemble the full product structure: PCBA, mechanical parts, harness, labels, packaging and literature, each at its correct level with quantities. This is the BOM procurement and production actually order against, so an omission here becomes a missing part at build. Reconcile the total against the costed budget and against the target COGS, and explain any variance rather than absorbing it silently.

steps.exitTrigger: Presentation or case study released
steps.entryQuestion: Is the client's approval obtained for anything externally visible?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the client approved the use of their name, images and any performance claim?
steps.whatToDo: Release the presentation or case study. Client approval is required for anything externally visible.
steps.guidelines: Produce the internal and, where permitted, external record of what was built and what problem it solved. Get client approval in writing for their name, product images and any performance figure before anything leaves the building — the contract usually restricts this and the restriction is routinely forgotten. Internally this becomes a capability reference for future proposals.

steps.exitTrigger: Product photography and video released to the project folder
steps.entryQuestion: Are the photographs of a unit that represents the released design?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the documented unit at the released revision, and is the client's approval on file?
steps.whatToDo: Add the photo and video assets, each labelled with the build revision it shows.
steps.guidelines: Photograph a unit at the released revision, not an early prototype with visible rework — reworked units in documentation cause avoidable questions from clients and auditors. Cover the assembled product, board top and bottom, enclosure detail and any assembly step worth recording. Store in the project folder; these images serve manuals, marketing and future service documentation.

steps.exitTrigger: User manual released
steps.entryQuestion: Does the manual describe how the product actually behaves rather than how it was intended to behave?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the manual been checked against the final firmware behaviour by someone who did not write it?
steps.whatToDo: Release the user manual against the released firmware and hardware revisions.
steps.guidelines: Write the manual against observed behaviour, not the specification — the two diverge during development and the manual is normally written from the specification because it is available earlier. Have someone follow it with the actual product and note every point where reality differs. Cover installation, first use, normal operation, indicators, fault conditions, maintenance and safety warnings.

steps.exitTrigger: Design learnings documented and fed into the Component Database
steps.entryQuestion: What would we do differently, and what proved reusable?
steps.exitQuestion: Has each learning changed a document — a checklist, a standard, a library entry?
steps.whatToDo: Add this project's design learnings while they are still fresh: what surprised you, what you would do differently, and what should become a standard.
steps.guidelines: Record what worked, what did not, and which blocks and parts are now proven enough to reuse. The test of a learning is whether it changed a document: a checklist item added, a design standard amended, a component promoted in the library. A learning that does not change a document will be relearned on the next project at the same cost.

steps.exitTrigger: Design for service review complete with findings recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Can this product be serviced, or is it disposable by design?
steps.exitQuestion: Can the failure-prone parts be replaced without destroying the product?
steps.whatToDo: Declare the service policy first, then judge every criterion against that policy. Set Result and Approval on every row.
steps.guidelines: Assess serviceability against the intended service model. Can the enclosure be opened without damage, can the board be removed, are the parts most likely to fail — connectors, batteries, electrolytics — replaceable? Is there diagnostic access after assembly? Where the product is intentionally not serviceable, record that as a decision rather than leaving it as an oversight, because it determines the warranty model.

steps.exitTrigger: Design for cost review complete with opportunities documented
steps.entryQuestion: Where is the cost concentrated, and which of it is design choice rather than requirement?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the BOM land within the target COGS, and if not, what specifically is driving the gap?
steps.whatToDo: Work through cost structure, design choice versus market price, and test and assembly cost. Every opportunity carries a rupee figure and an owner.
steps.guidelines: Rank the BOM by cost contribution and examine the top lines — cost is almost always concentrated in a handful of parts. For each, ask whether the cost is driven by a requirement or by a design choice made for convenience. Check layer count, board area, connector count and test time as well as parts. Opportunities identified here are still actionable; the same analysis after tooling is committed is a report, not a lever.

steps.exitTrigger: Design for environment review complete
steps.entryQuestion: Does the product meet the environmental obligations of its target markets?
steps.exitQuestion: Are RoHS, REACH, WEEE and packaging obligations all satisfied for the target markets?
steps.whatToDo: List every target market and its obligations, then evidence each one. A distributor's blanket statement is not a declaration for the part you bought.
steps.guidelines: Verify RoHS and REACH across the BOM, check WEEE and battery directive obligations where applicable, and assess packaging against recyclability requirements in the destination markets. Check disassembly for end-of-life material separation. These obligations are market-entry conditions rather than optional improvements, and discovering one late blocks shipment into that market entirely.

steps.exitTrigger: All DFx action items closed or formally waived
steps.entryQuestion: Does every finding across all DFx reviews have an owner, a target date and a disposition?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every open item either closed with evidence or carried in the waiver register with the right approver?
steps.whatToDo: Update every open row: owner, target date, disposition and what actually changed. A row still reading 'noted' is not closed.
steps.guidelines: Consolidate findings from every DFx review into one list with owner and target date against each. Close each with evidence of the change, not an assertion that it was addressed. Items that cannot be closed go to the waiver register with rationale, design authority and approver — and where the item is safety-derived, the customer approver is required because Elecbits cannot waive a safety-derived rule alone.

steps.entryTrigger: All DFx action items closed or waived
steps.exitTrigger: DFx sign-off obtained from all four stakeholder groups before fab release
steps.entryQuestion: Are Fab, EMS, Production and QA all satisfied with the design as it stands?
steps.exitQuestion: Has each of Fab, EMS, Production and QA signed, with any conditions recorded?
steps.whatToDo: Collect the four signatures — Fab, EMS, Production and QA — against the named file revision. A DFx sign-off by the designer alone is not a sign-off.
steps.guidelines: Obtain sign-off from Fab, EMS, Production and QA before fabrication release, not after. Each group is signing that they can execute their part with what has been provided. Conditions attached to a sign-off are recorded and tracked, not absorbed verbally. This is the gate that prevents a design being released to manufacturing that manufacturing has never actually reviewed.

steps.step: DFM/DFT Gate G2 review and sign-off
steps.entryTrigger: All DFx action items closed and DFx sign-off obtained from Fab, EMS, Production and QA
steps.exitTrigger: G2 released — build and test readiness confirmed with the EMS and the test owner against the Customer Extract view
steps.entryQuestion: Can this board be built and tested by the people who will actually build and test it?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the Dashboard show G2 as RELEASE, and has the EMS acknowledged the Customer Extract in writing?
steps.whatToDo: Confirm G2 shows RELEASE, share the Customer Extract view with the EMS and the fabricator, and record their written acknowledgement on the sign-off sheet.
steps.guidelines: G2 is where the file leaves the building. Share the Customer Extract view — the shared-visibility rows only — with the EMS and the fabricator, and get an acknowledgement back. Internal rows stay internal. A G2 signed without the EMS having seen it is a G2 signed by the wrong people.

steps.entryTrigger: G2 review held and all deviations identified
steps.exitTrigger: Every deviation recorded as a waiver with the required value, the actual value, the justification, the risk accepted and named approvers on both sides
steps.entryQuestion: What are we knowingly shipping outside our own rules, and who has accepted that risk by name?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every safety-derived waiver name the certification body that accepted it, and is every waiver status Accepted rather than Draft?
steps.whatToDo: Fill the Waivers tab: required value, actual value, justification, risk accepted and two named approvers per waiver. A safety-derived waiver also names the certification body.
steps.guidelines: Nothing gets deleted and nothing gets silently overridden. Every check that could not be met becomes a row on the Waivers tab with both numbers, the justification, the risk and two named approvers. A safety-derived waiver additionally names the certification body. A waiver still in Draft at fab release is an unaccepted risk being shipped, and it will be the first thing anyone asks about after a field failure.

steps.exitTrigger: Hardware section of the Audit Checklist populated with a link, a status, a date and an updater on every Required row
steps.entryQuestion: Is every hardware artefact named to convention and filed at its path in the sitemap?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every Required row in this section carry all four cells — Status, Link, Last updated and Updated by?
steps.whatToDo: Update the hardware section: block diagram, schematic, layout, Gerber, ODB, STEP, BOM, pick-and-place and the review record — each with Status, Link, Last updated and Updated by.
steps.guidelines: Paste the artefact filename into Links, set Status from the dropdown, stamp the date and record who updated it. Cover block diagram, schematic, layout, Gerber, ODB, STEP, BOM, pick-and-place and the design review record, each against its current revision. A row with a link but no status is an artefact nobody has accepted, and a status with no link is a claim with no evidence behind it.

steps.entryTrigger: DFx sign-off complete and all hardware artefacts released
steps.exitTrigger: Hardware release checklist closed and the track's outputs complete
steps.entryQuestion: Is every artefact on the hardware output pack present, versioned and stored correctly?
steps.exitQuestion: Are all thirteen output-pack artefacts present at consistent revisions in the project folder?
steps.whatToDo: Close the hardware section: every Required row carries all four cells, or the track is not released.
steps.guidelines: Close out the full hardware output pack: Gerber, Excellon and IPC-356, STEP, 3D PDF, project archive, BOM, pick and place, wiring document, conformal coating files and stencil, assembly drawing and instructions, product datasheet, design notes and design history. Verify every file is at a consistent revision and stored under the naming convention. This closure is the hardware track's exit into the merged Prototype stage.

steps.step: Test Environment Setup and Equipment Calibration
steps.entryTrigger: Hardware boards received from fab and assembled
steps.exitTrigger: Bench configured, instruments calibrated and the setup documented
steps.entryQuestion: Is every instrument the test plan calls for available and in calibration?
steps.exitQuestion: Could another engineer reproduce this bench from the document alone?
steps.whatToDo: Create the record and list every instrument the test plan calls for, its calibration date and its due date. An out-of-calibration instrument invalidates every result taken on it.
steps.guidelines: Record instrument make, model, serial and calibration due date for every piece of equipment on the bench, along with the probe and fixture configuration. Photograph the setup. An uncalibrated instrument turns every downstream measurement into an opinion, and a bench nobody can rebuild makes a failed retest impossible to argue about.

steps.exitTrigger: Electrical parameters, limits and tolerances agreed and frozen
steps.entryQuestion: Do the parameters trace back to the Testing Parameters agreed with the client at feasibility?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every parameter carry a target, an upper and a lower limit?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the parameter table: rail, target, minimum, maximum, method and the line in the client Testing Parameters it traces to.
steps.guidelines: List every rail, current draw, ripple, efficiency and protection threshold with a numeric target and both limits. Trace each one to the client-agreed Testing Parameters sheet so nothing is invented at test time. A parameter without a tolerance cannot fail, which means it also cannot pass.

steps.exitTrigger: Step-by-step electrical procedure written and reviewed
steps.entryQuestion: Is the sequence safe to run — is there a defined power-up order?
steps.exitQuestion: Can a technician run this without asking the designer a question?
steps.whatToDo: Create the procedure. Write it so a different engineer gets the same number: setup, connection, settings, sequence, and the pass criteria.
steps.guidelines: Write the procedure as ordered actions with the expected reading at each step, starting from a safe power-up sequence and current-limited supply. Name the instrument and the measurement point for every reading. The designer will not always be the person testing, and the first board is the worst one to improvise on.

steps.exitTrigger: Electrical test executed and measured values recorded against every parameter
steps.entryQuestion: Is the board visually inspected and continuity-checked before power is applied?
steps.exitQuestion: Is a measured number recorded against every parameter, including the ones that passed?
steps.whatToDo: Record the measured value for every parameter, not a tick. Enter the margin against the limit and attach the evidence file.
steps.guidelines: Execute the procedure exactly and record measured values, never tick marks. Note ambient conditions and supply configuration. Margin is the point of this step — a rail that passes at 3.28 V against a 3.3 V ±5% limit is a different board from one that reads 3.30 V, and only the number tells you which one you built.

steps.step: Power Integrity and Signal Integrity Measurement
steps.exitTrigger: PI and SI measurements captured on the identified critical nets
steps.entryQuestion: Which nets were flagged critical during simulation and layout review?
steps.exitQuestion: Do measured results agree with the simulation, and if not, is the divergence explained?
steps.whatToDo: Record the PI and SI measurements: ripple, droop, overshoot, eye and crosstalk, each against its target and its simulated prediction.
steps.guidelines: Measure ripple and transient response on each rail and eye diagrams or edge quality on the nets called out at layout review. Compare against the HyperLynx or Ansys results produced during design. Where measurement and simulation disagree, the disagreement is the finding — record it rather than discarding whichever number is less convenient.

steps.exitTrigger: Thermal images captured and hotspot temperatures logged at steady state
steps.entryQuestion: Is the board being run at a load that represents worst-case use?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every component sit inside its derating margin at steady state?
steps.whatToDo: Record the thermal survey: ambient, hot spots with component references, measured rise and the margin to each part's rating.
steps.guidelines: Run the board at worst-case load until temperatures stabilise, then capture thermal images and log the peak temperature of every component of concern against its rated maximum with the agreed derating margin applied. Test in free air and, where the enclosure exists, inside it — a board that passes on the bench and fails in its own case is a common and expensive discovery.

steps.step: Board-Level Functional Test Parameter and Procedure
steps.exitTrigger: Functional test parameters and procedure documented
steps.entryQuestion: Is every feature in the LLD represented by at least one functional test?
steps.exitQuestion: Are the pass criteria observable rather than subjective?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the board-level functional parameters and write the matching procedure. This is what the production test will later be built from.
steps.guidelines: Derive the functional cases directly from the feature list in the LLD so coverage is traceable rather than assumed. Every peripheral, interface and protection feature needs a case with an observable outcome. 'Works correctly' is not a pass criterion; 'LED turns red within 200 ms of the fault' is.

steps.exitTrigger: Functional test executed and results recorded per case
steps.entryQuestion: Is the correct firmware build loaded, and is its version recorded?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every functional case marked with a result and evidence?
steps.whatToDo: Record every functional result with its measured value, and log which board serial each result came from.
steps.guidelines: Record the firmware build hash alongside the results — a functional result is only meaningful against a known build. Capture evidence for failures with photographs or scope traces. Re-run the full set after any fix rather than only the case that failed, because fixes routinely break neighbours.

steps.exitTrigger: Environmental parameters and procedure documented
steps.entryQuestion: What temperature, humidity and vibration profile does the deployment actually see?
steps.exitQuestion: Do the profiles reflect real conditions rather than laboratory convenience?
steps.whatToDo: Populate the environmental parameters: standard, severity level, duration, and the pass criteria for each.
steps.guidelines: Set the profile from the real deployment environment described in the client questionnaire, not from a default chamber recipe. State soak durations and ramp rates. A product destined for a rooftop in Rajasthan and one destined for an air-conditioned panel do not share a test profile, and pretending they do is how field failures are designed in.

steps.exitTrigger: Environmental testing executed and results recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Is the chamber programme verified before the run starts?
steps.exitQuestion: Did the board remain functional throughout, and was it retested after return to ambient?
steps.whatToDo: Record the environmental results including the chamber profile actually run, not just the one specified.
steps.guidelines: Run the profile with the board powered and monitored so intermittent faults are caught while they happen rather than inferred afterwards. Functionally retest after return to ambient. A unit that survives the chamber but fails afterwards has a latent defect, and that is exactly the failure the chamber exists to find.

steps.exitTrigger: Burn-in completed for the agreed duration with results logged
steps.entryQuestion: Is the burn-in duration and sample size agreed for this build stage?
steps.exitQuestion: Did any unit drift or fail during the run, and was the cause established?
steps.whatToDo: Record the burn-in: duration, ambient, load, unit count, and every failure with its hour of failure.
steps.guidelines: Run 24 to 72 hours at elevated temperature under representative load with periodic functional checks logged, not just a pass at the end. Infant mortality shows up here or it shows up at the customer. Record drift as well as failure, because a parameter walking steadily in one direction is a finding even when it never crosses the limit.

steps.step: Hardware Defect Log and Root Cause Analysis
steps.exitTrigger: Every defect closed with a root cause and a disposition
steps.entryQuestion: Is each failure logged with the board serial, the build revision and the conditions?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every defect carry a root cause, a corrective action and a verification result?
steps.whatToDo: Log every defect against the board revision and the process used, with root cause and disposition. A defect with no root cause will happen again.
steps.guidelines: Log every defect against board serial and revision, then drive each to a root cause rather than a replacement part. Record the disposition — fix now, fix at next revision, or accept with justification — and verify the fix by retest. This log is the input to the next revision and to the design history; without it, the same fault is rediscovered on the next project.

steps.exitTrigger: Hardware test reports issued for every applicable test family
steps.entryQuestion: Are the electrical and board-level test parameters available to test against?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every parameter defined at feasibility have a measured result recorded against it?
steps.whatToDo: Assemble the hardware test report: link the parameters, the procedure and the results for every test family. All three, not just the report.
steps.guidelines: Issue the hardware test reports against the parameters set at feasibility — electrical, board-level functional, thermal and reliability. Every test family follows the same three-artefact rule: a parameter document, a procedure document, and the test-and-report. Record measured values, not pass marks; a pass without a number cannot be compared across builds and tells you nothing about margin.

steps.step: Audit Checklist update — Hardware test evidence
steps.exitTrigger: Hardware test rows in the Audit Checklist carry measured evidence and an approval status
steps.entryQuestion: Are all hardware test reports complete with measured values rather than pass marks?
steps.exitQuestion: Is each test row linked to its parameter document, procedure document and report?
steps.whatToDo: Update the hardware test rows with measured evidence, linking parameters, procedure and report for each family.
steps.guidelines: Link all three artefacts per test family — parameters, procedure and report — not just the report. The checklist is the only place the three are visibly tied together, and a report whose parameters cannot be located cannot be defended when a result is later questioned.

steps.entryTrigger: Designer LLD locked and hardware block diagram in draft
steps.exitTrigger: Firmware system block diagram drafted showing layers and external interfaces
steps.entryQuestion: Is the firmware scope defined — which functions live in firmware versus hardware?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the diagram show all five architectural layers and every external interface?
steps.whatToDo: Create the firmware block diagram: every module, every interface between them, and where each one gets its data.
steps.guidelines: Draw the firmware architecture as layers: L0 hardware, L1 vendor SDK, L2 HAL, L3 middleware components, L4 application. Show every external interface — sensors, radios, storage, cloud — and which layer owns it. The rules are structural: layers call downward only, the application never includes a vendor header, and hardware specifics live only in board_config.h. A diagram that violates the layering is a design that will not port to the next product.

steps.step: Block diagram review with checklist - 1st review - self
steps.exitTrigger: Self-review complete with layering violations corrected
steps.entryQuestion: Has the author checked the diagram against the architecture rules personally?
steps.exitQuestion: Does any module call upward, or include a vendor header above L1?
steps.whatToDo: Self-review the firmware block diagram against the LLD. Set Result, Approval and Checked by on every criterion.
steps.guidelines: Check your own diagram against the layering rules before review. The specific things to look for are upward calls, vendor headers appearing above L1, and hardware specifics leaking outside board_config.h. These are the violations that make firmware unportable, and they are far cheaper to fix on a diagram than in a codebase.

steps.step: Block diagram review with checklist - 2nd review
steps.exitTrigger: Second review complete with findings logged and closed
steps.entryQuestion: Is a second firmware reviewer available who did not author the design?
steps.exitQuestion: Have reuse opportunities from fw-core been identified rather than reimplemented?
steps.whatToDo: Independent second review by someone who did not draw it.
steps.guidelines: Independent review against the architecture checklist. Beyond correctness, look for what should be reused: if a component exists in fw-core it is pinned by tag, never copied in. Reuse percentage against new products is a tracked metric with a 60–80% target, and it is decided at this review, not later. Mahesh is the firmware authority where a design point is disputed.

steps.exitTrigger: Joint review complete with the hardware-firmware interface agreed
steps.entryQuestion: Has the hardware block diagram been shared and read?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every peripheral, pin and boot dependency agreed and written down?
steps.whatToDo: Add the joint review with hardware: peripheral map, pin usage and timing assumptions agreed and written down.
steps.guidelines: Convergence point with the hardware track. Agree the peripheral map, pin allocation, boot mode strategy, debug interface and reset behaviour. Firmware must state what it needs — a spare UART for logging, a GPIO for a watchdog kick, boot straps accessible after assembly — while those are still free changes on a schematic. Record the agreement; it is the interface contract both tracks build against.

steps.exitTrigger: State machine drafted covering boot through fault handling
steps.entryQuestion: Are all operating modes and transitions between them identified?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every state have a defined exit for both success and failure?
steps.whatToDo: Create the state machine: every state, every transition, its trigger, and what happens on an unexpected input. Unhandled transitions are where field bugs live.
steps.guidelines: Chart the full lifecycle: boot, provision, connect, operate, OTA, fault, recover. Every state needs defined entry and exit conditions and a defined behaviour on failure — unhandled failure transitions are where field devices go unresponsive and require a site visit. Include timeouts on every waiting state. This document is written before coding, not derived from it afterwards.

steps.step: State Machine diagram/Flow Chart - 1st review - self
steps.exitTrigger: Self-review complete with unreachable states and dead ends removed
steps.entryQuestion: Has every state and transition been traced through personally?
steps.exitQuestion: Is any state unreachable, and can any state be entered with no route out?
steps.whatToDo: Self-review the state machine against the LLD: every behaviour represented, no unreachable state, no state with no exit.
steps.guidelines: Trace every path yourself. Look specifically for unreachable states, states with no exit, and transitions that lack a timeout. A state that can be entered but not left is a device that requires a power cycle, and in a deployed product that means a truck roll. Check that power loss at any point leaves the device in a recoverable state.

steps.exitTrigger: Second review complete with findings closed
steps.entryQuestion: Is the reviewer familiar with the product's real operating environment?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the machine handle network loss, power loss and sensor failure at every state?
steps.whatToDo: Record the second-pass state machine review and the findings raised.
steps.guidelines: Review against real-world failure modes rather than the happy path: network loss mid-transaction, power loss mid-write, a sensor returning implausible values, an OTA interrupted at the worst moment. The happy path is rarely where firmware fails. Log findings and re-verify after correction.

steps.exitTrigger: State machine released as a versioned baseline
steps.entryQuestion: Are all findings closed and the version incremented?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the released diagram stored in the project folder under the naming convention?
steps.whatToDo: Record the released revision of the state machine and flowchart in the FDD, with the date and the approver.
steps.guidelines: Release as a frozen, versioned baseline. The state machine and the logic sheet together form the seed of the test specification — the test cases are derived from the states and transitions, so a released state machine is what makes systematic firmware testing possible. Any behaviour change after release updates this document as part of the same change, not afterwards.

steps.entryTrigger: State machine released and MCU confirmed
steps.exitTrigger: Memory map defined with partitions sized and documented
steps.entryQuestion: Are flash and RAM budgets known for application, bootloader, OTA and storage?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the OTA scheme fit within available flash with room for rollback?
steps.whatToDo: Add the memory map: flash and RAM partitioning, bootloader region, application region, storage region and what survives an update.
steps.guidelines: Partition flash for bootloader, application, OTA staging and persistent storage, and size each with headroom. The OTA scheme drives this most: dual-bank requires roughly twice the application space and running out of it late forces either a redesign or the removal of rollback, which is not an acceptable trade. Define the RAM budget including worst-case stack and heap. Record the map; it constrains every subsequent decision.

steps.exitTrigger: Logic sheet drafted covering all functional behaviour
steps.entryQuestion: Is every functional behaviour specified precisely enough to implement and to test?
steps.exitQuestion: Could a test engineer write test cases from this document without asking questions?
steps.whatToDo: Create the internal logic sheet: every behaviour with its trigger, condition, action and timing, written so it can be tested.
steps.guidelines: The logic sheet is the signed contract between PM, hardware and firmware — it states exactly what the product does under every condition, with thresholds, timings and precedence made explicit. Write it so a test engineer can derive test cases directly from it. Where behaviour depends on configuration, state the default and the permitted range. This is the document that resolves 'is that a bug or is that intended' arguments.

steps.exitTrigger: Self-review complete with gaps and contradictions corrected
steps.entryQuestion: Has every behaviour been checked against the LLD and the state machine?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every threshold, timeout and precedence rule stated numerically?
steps.whatToDo: Self-review the logic sheet against the LLD and the state machine, looking specifically for contradictions between the two.
steps.guidelines: Check the logic sheet against the LLD and the state machine for gaps and contradictions. Every threshold, timeout and priority needs a number — 'reconnects quickly' is not implementable and not testable. Look for behaviours that are described in one document and contradicted in another; that contradiction will be resolved by whoever writes the code, silently.

steps.exitTrigger: Second review complete with PM and hardware agreement
steps.entryQuestion: Have PM and hardware both reviewed the behaviour this commits to?
steps.exitQuestion: Do PM, hardware and firmware all agree this is what the product does?
steps.whatToDo: Record the second-pass logic sheet review and every gap it found.
steps.guidelines: This review is cross-functional because the logic sheet is a cross-functional contract. PM confirms it matches what was sold; hardware confirms it is achievable with the designed circuit; firmware confirms it is implementable. Disagreement discovered here is a conversation. Discovered at validation it is a rework of code, tests and often the client relationship.

steps.entryTrigger: Reviews closed and cross-functional agreement reached
steps.exitTrigger: Logic sheet released as the signed behavioural baseline
steps.entryQuestion: Are all findings closed and the version incremented?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the released version stored and referenced by the test specification?
steps.whatToDo: Create the customer-facing logic sheet from the internal one: the behaviour the client agreed to, without the internal implementation detail.
steps.guidelines: Release as the signed baseline. From this point a pull request that changes behaviour without updating the logic sheet is rejected — that rule is what keeps the document true, and a logic sheet that has silently drifted from the code is worse than none because it is trusted. The test specification is written against this version.

steps.entryTrigger: Trial hardware ordered at the pre-design stage
steps.exitTrigger: Trial hardware received, inspected and logged against the project
steps.entryQuestion: Has the received hardware been checked against what was ordered?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the received hardware the correct part and revision for this design?
steps.whatToDo: Log the trial hardware received into R&D inventory: board revision, serial, quantity and who holds each unit.
steps.guidelines: Check what arrived against what was ordered — dev board revisions differ in ways that matter, particularly pin availability and onboard peripherals. Log receipt against the project. If the wrong revision arrived, raise it immediately; the firmware track is blocked without working hardware and the lead time to correct it is the same as the original order.

steps.exitTrigger: Dev board setup working with basic peripheral access verified
steps.entryQuestion: Is the target MCU and its peripheral set represented well enough to develop against?
steps.exitQuestion: Can the setup exercise every peripheral the final design will use?
steps.whatToDo: Create the setup guide and document the dev board configuration: jumpers, straps, power source and known differences from the target board.
steps.guidelines: Assemble a bench setup that represents the real design as closely as possible: same MCU family, the actual sensors and radios where available, representative power arrangement. Verify each peripheral responds before building on top of it. Development against a setup that differs materially from the target produces firmware that works on the bench and fails on the first article, and the difference is usually discovered slowly.

steps.entryTrigger: Project started and target MCU confirmed
steps.exitTrigger: Toolchain configured, containerised and building the reference project
steps.entryQuestion: Is the toolchain version pinned and reproducible across every engineer?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the project build identically on another engineer's machine and in CI?
steps.whatToDo: Add the toolchain: IDE version, compiler version, build flags and any patch. A build that only works on one laptop is not a build.
steps.guidelines: Pin the toolchain version and put it in the standard container for the platform. Everyone builds in the container; building outside it is unsupported. This is not process for its own sake — an unpinned toolchain means the binary that passed testing cannot be reproduced, which makes a field failure impossible to investigate. Verify the reference project builds byte-identically in CI and on a second machine.

steps.exitTrigger: Programming and flashing verified end to end
steps.entryQuestion: Is the programming interface accessible on both dev board and target design?
steps.exitQuestion: Can the target be flashed and recovered from a bad image?
steps.whatToDo: Add the programmer and flasher setup: hardware, driver, settings and the exact command that programs a blank part.
steps.guidelines: Verify programming works on both the dev setup and the intended target, including recovery from a failed or corrupt image. Confirm the debug and programming header is accessible on the real board after assembly and, where relevant, after the enclosure is fitted — a debug header that a production board cannot reach removes the only route to diagnosing a returned unit. Document the procedure.

steps.exitTrigger: Debug and monitoring tooling operational
steps.entryQuestion: Are logging, tracing and runtime monitoring available on the target?
steps.exitQuestion: Can heap, stack and timing be observed on the target while it runs?
steps.whatToDo: Add the debug and monitoring setup: interface, baud, log format and how to capture a trace when something fails at three in the morning.
steps.guidelines: Set up logging output, debugger connection and any runtime monitoring for heap, stack and timing. Log levels are configurable at build so production images can be quiet without a separate code path. Heap and stack observation matters specifically because the failures that appear after 48 hours of soak — fragmentation, slow leaks, stack growth on a rare path — are invisible without it.

steps.entryTrigger: Development environment ready and architecture agreed
steps.exitTrigger: fw-core components identified and pinned by tag
steps.entryQuestion: Which required functions already exist in fw-core?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every reused component pinned by tag rather than copied into the product repo?
steps.whatToDo: Record which universal repo functions are being reused, at which release tag, and what was modified locally.
steps.guidelines: Search fw-core before writing anything: logging, error codes, ring buffers, CRC, state machine helpers, key-value store, watchdog, AT engine, modem drivers, Wi-Fi manager, MQTT, telemetry, OTA, provisioning. Pin by tag — a file copied into the product repo forks silently and never receives the fix that was made upstream. Reuse percentage is a tracked metric with a 60–80% target for new products.

steps.exitTrigger: Module tests passing in CI at the required coverage
steps.entryQuestion: Does each module have host-side unit tests covering its logic?
steps.exitQuestion: Do the tests run in CI rather than only on a developer machine?
steps.whatToDo: Record the module test results: which modules, which cases, coverage achieved against target, and every failing case.
steps.guidelines: Write host-side unit tests for logic-bearing modules — state machines, parsers, buffer handling — using the standard framework. Stable shared components carry a coverage target of at least 70%. Tests run in CI on every push; tests that only run locally decay within weeks and provide false assurance. Include boundary conditions and error injection, not only the expected path.

steps.exitTrigger: Code review complete with findings addressed and PR merged
steps.entryQuestion: Does the code follow the coding standard and the layering rules?
steps.exitQuestion: Have two reviewers approved anything destined for fw-core?
steps.whatToDo: Record the static analysis run and the code review findings together: tool version, rule set, warning count, and every warning suppressed with its reason.
steps.guidelines: Review against the coding standard and the reliability rules, enforced by clang-format and static analysis in pre-commit and CI so review time goes to logic rather than formatting. One reviewer for product repositories, two for fw-core, because fw-core defects propagate to every product. A pull request that changes behaviour without updating the logic sheet or README is rejected.

steps.exitTrigger: Product-level firmware testing complete against the logic sheet
steps.entryQuestion: Is the complete firmware running on representative hardware?
steps.exitQuestion: Does observed behaviour match the logic sheet in every state and transition?
steps.whatToDo: Record on-target testing at product level: what ran on real hardware, on which board revision, and what differed from the host results.
steps.guidelines: Test the integrated firmware against the logic sheet state by state and transition by transition. Include the release checklist items: a thousand-cycle power-cycle loop, network-loss recovery, watchdog fire and recover, and a 48-hour soak with heap monitoring. These four find the defects that unit tests structurally cannot, because they are about accumulation and interruption rather than logic.

steps.exitTrigger: Integrated build produced with git hash embedded
steps.entryQuestion: Are all feature branches merged and is the build clean?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the binary report its git hash at boot?
steps.whatToDo: Update the FDD to match the integrated source: final module list, interfaces and any deviation from the design as originally written.
steps.guidelines: Merge to the release branch and produce the integrated build through CI. The git hash is baked into the binary and printed at boot — this is what makes a returned unit diagnosable, because 'which build is this' is otherwise unanswerable. No field or client unit is ever flashed with a laptop build; every deployed binary comes from CI with a traceable hash.

steps.exitTrigger: Final review complete with all findings closed
steps.entryQuestion: Has the full codebase been reviewed, not only the incremental changes?
steps.exitQuestion: Have safety-critical and security-relevant paths had line-by-line review?
steps.whatToDo: Record the final code review: reviewer, scope, findings and their disposition. A review with no findings is a review that did not happen.
steps.guidelines: Review the integrated whole, not just the diffs — integration introduces interactions that incremental review does not see. Give safety-critical and security-relevant paths line-by-line attention. Check static analysis output is clean, error handling is complete on every return path, and no debug or test hooks remain enabled in the release configuration.

steps.entryTrigger: Final review closed and all tests passing
steps.exitTrigger: Firmware released with tag, changelog and binary archived
steps.entryQuestion: Is the release tagged, the changelog written and the artefact archived?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the released binary reproducible from the tagged source in the container?
steps.whatToDo: Record the release in the FDD: version, git tag, build hash and the binary's checksum. The hash is what makes a build reproducible.
steps.guidelines: Tag the release using semantic versioning, write the changelog, and archive the binary with its build metadata against the project ID. Verify the binary is reproducible from the tag in the standard container — a release that cannot be rebuilt is a release that cannot be supported. Link the firmware version to the PCB revision it targets.

steps.entryTrigger: Application firmware released and test parameters defined
steps.exitTrigger: Production test firmware released with pass/fail criteria defined
steps.entryQuestion: What must the production line be able to verify on every unit?
steps.exitQuestion: Does it exercise every interface the board-level test parameters require, with automatic pass/fail?
steps.template: Firmware Test Hooks and Diagnostic Command Set
steps.whatToDo: Add the production and diagnostic firmware detail: how it is entered, what it exposes, and how it differs from the shipping build.
steps.guidelines: Build the firmware the production line flashes to verify a board before the application is loaded. It exercises every interface in the board-level functional test parameters and returns an unambiguous pass or fail with a failure code — a test requiring operator interpretation produces inconsistent results between shifts. Record results per serial number. This is a real deliverable with its own version, not a bench script.

steps.entryTrigger: Production test and application firmware released
steps.exitTrigger: Code upload procedure reviewed and validated by someone outside the firmware team
steps.entryQuestion: Does the document let a line operator flash a unit correctly without firmware support?
steps.exitQuestion: Has a non-firmware person successfully followed it end to end?
steps.whatToDo: Check the uploading process document: can a line operator flash a board correctly from this alone, with no engineer present?
steps.guidelines: The document covers hardware connection, tool versions, file names and their locations, flashing sequence, verification and troubleshooting. Test it by having someone outside the firmware team follow it — the assumptions a firmware engineer does not know they are making are exactly what stops the line. Include what to do when flashing fails.

steps.exitTrigger: Code upload document released to production
steps.entryQuestion: Are the correct binary versions referenced with their hashes?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the document name the exact binary versions and where they are stored?
steps.whatToDo: Release the uploading process document against the released firmware version.
steps.guidelines: Release with exact binary versions, hashes and storage locations named. Ambiguity about which file to flash produces units in the field running an unintended build, and that is discovered months later during a support call. Include the sequence where production test firmware is flashed, the test run, and the application firmware then loaded.

steps.exitTrigger: Firmware section of the Audit Checklist populated with a link, a status, a date and an updater on every Required row
steps.entryQuestion: Is every firmware artefact named to convention and filed at its path in the sitemap?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every Required row in this section carry all four cells — Status, Link, Last updated and Updated by?
steps.whatToDo: Update the firmware section: architecture, block diagram, state machine, flowchart, logic sheet, release tag and build hash.
steps.guidelines: Paste the artefact filename into Links, set Status from the dropdown, stamp the date and record who updated it. Cover architecture, block diagram, state machine, flowchart, logic sheet, source release tag and build hash. A row with a link but no status is an artefact nobody has accepted, and a status with no link is a claim with no evidence behind it.

steps.step: Firmware DFT — diagnostic command set and test hooks
steps.entryTrigger: Firmware architecture frozen and board-level functional test parameters known
steps.exitTrigger: Diagnostic command set documented — every functional test parameter readable over one interface at a fixed baud
steps.entryQuestion: Can the production test read every parameter it needs from firmware, without a bench instrument at the station?
steps.exitQuestion: Is there a documented command for every functional test parameter, and is the interface locked against use in the field?
steps.template: Firmware Test Hooks and Diagnostic Command Set
steps.whatToDo: Populate the command table: one row per functional test parameter, with the exact command string, the exact response format, the unit and the range. Fix the interface and the baud.
steps.guidelines: Every parameter that only an oscilloscope or a multimeter can see is a fixture cost and a cycle-time cost. Walk the board-level functional test parameter list and write a diagnostic command for each one. Fix the interface and the baud so the production script never has to auto-detect. Then make sure the same interface cannot be reached by an end user — locked, fused, or behind a sequence that normal use will never produce.

steps.exitTrigger: Programming method, provisioning data set, serial and key source of truth, and the cycle-time budget all defined and proven on real hardware
steps.entryQuestion: How does a blank board become a serialised, provisioned, locked unit — and how long does that take per unit?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the measured cycle inside the budget, and is a unit that fails mid-provisioning still recoverable at the station?
steps.whatToDo: Create the plan and write the order of operations: erase, write, verify, provision, self-test, then lock. The lock step goes last so a failed unit is still recoverable.
steps.guidelines: Write down the order of operations: erase, write, verify, provision, self-test, then lock. The lock or fuse step goes last so a failed unit is still recoverable. Name who allocates serials, MACs and keys, where they are recorded, and what happens to a unit that fails after a key has been issued. Measure the cycle on real hardware — an estimate here becomes a second test station later.

steps.exitTrigger: Firmware release checklist closed and the track's outputs complete
steps.entryQuestion: Is every item on the firmware release checklist verified?
steps.exitQuestion: Are the power-cycle, network-loss, watchdog and soak tests all evidenced?
steps.whatToDo: Close the firmware section: every Required row carries Status, Link, Last updated and Updated by.
steps.guidelines: Close the release checklist with evidence, not assertion: the thousand-cycle power-cycle loop, network-loss recovery, watchdog fire and recover, and the 48-hour soak with heap monitoring each need a result recorded. Confirm all documentation is released and the Component Index is updated. This closure is the firmware track's exit into the merged Prototype stage.

steps.entryTrigger: New reusable functions developed during this project
steps.exitTrigger: New components registered in the Component Index with owner and maturity
steps.entryQuestion: Which functions written here are reusable beyond this product?
steps.exitQuestion: Does each entry carry an owner, a maturity grade and a README with API and footprint?
steps.whatToDo: Register the new reusable functions this project produced, with their interface and their intended reuse scope.
steps.guidelines: Register genuinely reusable functions in the Component Index with name, purpose, supported platforms, maturity grade, owner, memory footprint and documentation link. A component is Done when it compiles on all declared platforms, has host unit tests in CI, has a README with API and limitations, has a working example, is indexed with an owner, and has been reviewed by two people. Anything short of that is product code, not a component.

steps.step: Firmware Test Plan and Coverage Targets
steps.exitTrigger: Test plan approved with coverage targets stated per layer
steps.entryQuestion: Are the four test layers scoped — host unit, on-target, integration and system?
steps.exitQuestion: Is a numeric coverage target set for logic in Stable components?
steps.whatToDo: Create the test plan: scope per layer, coverage targets, the environment each layer runs in, and what constitutes done.
steps.guidelines: Define what is tested at each of the four layers and set a numeric coverage target — at least 70% logic coverage for anything graded Stable. State explicitly what will not be tested and why. An untested path is acceptable when it is a recorded decision and dangerous when it is an oversight.

steps.exitTrigger: Unit tests executed in CI with coverage report produced
steps.entryQuestion: Do the unit tests run in CI rather than only on a developer machine?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the coverage figure at or above target, and is the report attached?
steps.whatToDo: Record the host unit test run: cases, pass and fail counts, coverage achieved, and every case excluded with its reason.
steps.guidelines: Run the unit suite through CI so the result is reproducible and attributable to a commit, with the HAL mocked so logic is tested independently of hardware. Attach the coverage report. A green run on someone's laptop proves that laptop works, which is not the claim being made.

steps.exitTrigger: Static analysis executed and every finding triaged
steps.entryQuestion: Are the analysis rules configured and agreed for this codebase?
steps.exitQuestion: Has every warning been fixed, suppressed with justification, or accepted with a reason?
steps.whatToDo: Record the static analysis: tool, rule set, findings by severity, and the disposition of each.
steps.guidelines: Run cppcheck or clang-tidy against the agreed rule set and triage every finding — fixed, suppressed with a written reason, or accepted. An unexamined warning list is worse than no analysis, because it creates the appearance of rigour while hiding the one warning that mattered.

steps.exitTrigger: HAL and module tests executed on real hardware
steps.entryQuestion: Is the target board available at the correct revision?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every HAL function behave on hardware as its host mock does?
steps.whatToDo: Record HAL and module testing on target: board revision, firmware version and results per module.
steps.guidelines: Exercise each HAL function on the real board and compare behaviour against the mock used in unit testing. Divergence between mock and metal is the defect this layer exists to find, and it is always cheaper to find here than during integration.

steps.entryTrigger: Hardware functional testing passed and firmware on target
steps.exitTrigger: Integration test executed across every hardware and firmware interface
steps.entryQuestion: Is the interface definition from the LLD available to test against?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every peripheral, interrupt and protocol interface behave to the logic sheet?
steps.whatToDo: Record hardware-software integration results: which interfaces were exercised together and what broke at the boundary.
steps.guidelines: Test against the logic sheet, which is the signed contract between PM, hardware and firmware — if behaviour and logic sheet disagree, one of them is wrong and the discrepancy must be resolved rather than absorbed. Cover every interrupt, every bus and every timing-sensitive path.

steps.exitTrigger: HIL smoke suite green on the reference board
steps.entryQuestion: Is the reference board wired to the HIL shelf and is the smoke script current?
steps.exitQuestion: Did power-cycle, network-loss recovery and watchdog recovery all pass?
steps.whatToDo: Record the HIL smoke run: rig configuration, cases, and the results against the expected behaviour.
steps.guidelines: Run the automated smoke suite on the shelf with relay power switching and UART capture so results are machine-produced rather than observed. This is the regression net — it is what stops a fix in one area silently breaking recovery behaviour in another, which is the failure mode that reaches the field undetected.

steps.exitTrigger: Boundary and fault-injection cases executed with behaviour recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Are the boundary values and fault modes enumerated from the design?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the device fail safe and recover predictably under every injected fault?
steps.whatToDo: Record boundary and fault-injection testing: the boundary values and fault modes enumerated from the design, and what the product actually did.
steps.guidelines: Push inputs to their limits and beyond, inject the faults the design claims to handle — sensor disconnect, corrupt payload, memory exhaustion, network drop — and record what actually happens. Handling a fault gracefully is a design claim; this step is where the claim is either evidenced or withdrawn.

steps.exitTrigger: OTA update, interruption and rollback all tested and evidenced
steps.entryQuestion: Is the OTA path the one that will be used in production, including signing?
steps.exitQuestion: Does an interrupted update recover to a working image every time?
steps.whatToDo: Record OTA and recovery testing including the interrupted-update case. A unit that bricks mid-update is the failure that matters.
steps.guidelines: Test the production OTA path with production signing, then deliberately interrupt updates at several points — mid-download, mid-write, during the bank switch — and confirm rollback every time. A bricked unit in the field costs a site visit; the same failure caught here costs an afternoon.

steps.exitTrigger: Soak completed with heap and power traces logged
steps.entryQuestion: Are the sleep, wake and low-power transitions enumerated for this product?
steps.exitQuestion: Did the 48-hour soak complete with no heap growth and no unexplained reset?
steps.whatToDo: Record the soak: duration, power-mode transitions exercised, drift observed and any leak or lock-up.
steps.guidelines: Exercise every power-mode transition and run the 48-hour soak with heap monitoring and reset logging. A slow leak is invisible in a ten-minute test and fatal in a device meant to run for months, and this is the only step in the process designed to catch it.

steps.step: Firmware Defect Log and Root Cause Analysis
steps.exitTrigger: Every defect closed with root cause, fix commit and retest result
steps.entryQuestion: Is each defect logged against a build hash and a reproducible case?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every defect link to the commit that fixed it and the test that proved it?
steps.whatToDo: Log every firmware defect with the build it was found on, its root cause and the commit that fixed it.
steps.guidelines: Log defects against the build hash with a reproduction case, and link each to the fixing commit and the retest that closed it. Keep the reproduction case in the test suite afterwards. A bug fixed without a regression test is a bug scheduled to return.

steps.exitTrigger: Firmware test reports issued covering all four test layers
steps.entryQuestion: Are unit, module and product-level test results all available?
steps.exitQuestion: Are coverage figures, soak results and recovery test outcomes all evidenced?
steps.whatToDo: Assemble the firmware test report linking plan, execution and results per layer.
steps.guidelines: Issue reports across the four layers: host unit tests with coverage figures, on-target HAL tests, hardware-in-the-loop smoke results, and the release checklist outcomes. Include the power-cycle loop, network-loss recovery, watchdog behaviour and the 48-hour soak with heap trace. Static analysis output belongs here too, since a clean run is evidence and an unexamined warning list is not.

steps.step: Audit Checklist update — Firmware test evidence
steps.exitTrigger: Firmware test rows in the Audit Checklist carry measured evidence and an approval status
steps.entryQuestion: Are all firmware test reports complete with measured values rather than pass marks?
steps.exitQuestion: Is each test row linked to its parameter document, procedure document and report?
steps.whatToDo: Update the firmware test rows with the evidence: plan, procedure and report for each layer.
steps.guidelines: Link all three artefacts per test family — parameters, procedure and report — not just the report. The checklist is the only place the three are visibly tied together, and a report whose parameters cannot be located cannot be defended when a result is later questioned.

steps.entryTrigger: Designer LLD locked and product form factor defined
steps.exitTrigger: Features checklist completed across all eight consideration areas
steps.entryQuestion: Are the user, environmental and mechanical requirements all captured?
steps.exitQuestion: Has every one of the eight areas been addressed or explicitly marked not applicable?
steps.whatToDo: Create the EDD and complete the features checklist: every user-facing feature, ingress requirement, mounting method and material constraint.
steps.guidelines: Complete the checklist across its eight areas: user and product considerations, enclosure dimensions, thermal, IP rating strategy, material and manufacturing process selection, tolerance stack-up, logo and marking artwork, and CMF. Each drives downstream decisions that are expensive to revisit — the IP strategy determines sealing and therefore the whole parting-line design, and the manufacturing process determines draft, wall thickness and minimum radii before any surface is drawn.

steps.exitTrigger: First concept sketched and rendered
steps.entryQuestion: Is there enough requirement definition to explore form?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the concept satisfy the dimensional envelope and the IP strategy?
steps.whatToDo: Add concept 1 with its rationale: what it optimises for and what it gives up.
steps.guidelines: Explore form against the constraint set rather than in the abstract: dimensional envelope, mounting method, user interaction points, ingress strategy. Sketch, then render in Keyshot to make it discussable with non-designers. A concept that ignores the constraints produces an attractive review and a wasted week, because the constraints do not move.

steps.exitTrigger: Second concept produced offering a genuine alternative
steps.entryQuestion: Does an alternative approach deserve exploration before converging?
steps.exitQuestion: Do the two concepts differ meaningfully rather than cosmetically?
steps.whatToDo: Add concept 2 as a genuine alternative, not a variation. Two concepts that differ only in fillet radius is one concept.
steps.guidelines: Produce a second concept that differs structurally — a different split line, assembly method, or thermal approach — not a colour variation. Two concepts that differ only cosmetically give the reviewer no real choice and waste the review. The comparison is what surfaces which constraints are actually binding.

steps.exitTrigger: Concept review complete with one direction selected
steps.entryQuestion: Have both concepts been assessed against the full features checklist?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the selected concept satisfy every checklist item, or are the exceptions recorded?
steps.whatToDo: Record the concept review against the features checklist. Set Result and Approval per criterion and name the checker.
steps.guidelines: Review both concepts against the features checklist item by item and select a direction with the reasoning recorded. Check manufacturability at concept stage — draft, wall thickness, undercuts, minimum radii — because a concept that cannot be moulded is discovered at tooling quotation, by which point the client has usually seen and approved the render.

steps.exitTrigger: Joint concept review complete with hardware agreement
steps.entryQuestion: Has hardware seen the internal volume, mounting and thermal implications?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the concept give hardware the board area, height and thermal path it needs?
steps.whatToDo: Add the concept review with hardware: internal volume, board mounting, connector alignment and the thermal path.
steps.guidelines: Convergence point with the hardware track. Confirm the internal volume supports the board area and component heights, that mounting is compatible with the intended board outline, that connectors reach their apertures, and that the thermal path works. Hardware commits to a board outline from this; enclosure commits to an internal envelope. Both are then constrained, which is the point.

steps.exitTrigger: CAD model built with manufacturing rules applied
steps.entryQuestion: Are the manufacturing process and material selected so the model can respect their rules?
steps.exitQuestion: Are draft angles, wall thicknesses and radii consistent with the selected process?
steps.whatToDo: Record the CAD modelling decisions: wall sections, draft, rib strategy, boss design and the parting line.
steps.guidelines: Build the model with the process rules applied from the first feature: uniform wall thickness, draft on every vertical face, generous radii, ribs at the correct proportion of wall thickness. Model parametrically so downstream changes propagate. A model built without draft has to be substantially rebuilt when tooling is quoted, and that rebuild invalidates every fit check already done against it.

steps.exitTrigger: CAD review complete with findings corrected
steps.entryQuestion: Has the model been checked against the mechanical design checklist?
steps.exitQuestion: Are there undercuts, insufficient draft or wall thickness variations that will not mould?
steps.whatToDo: Record the CAD review against the checklist, criterion by criterion.
steps.guidelines: Review against the checklist: draft, wall thickness uniformity, undercuts, radii, boss and rib proportions, parting line, ejection. Run the moulding analysis tools where available. These are cheap to correct in CAD, expensive to correct in steel, and impossible to correct once the tool is cut without a tool modification and its schedule.

steps.exitTrigger: Joint CAD review complete with internal geometry agreed
steps.entryQuestion: Has hardware confirmed the internal geometry against the current board layout?
steps.exitQuestion: Do standoffs, bosses and keep-outs match the current board revision?
steps.whatToDo: Add the CAD review with hardware, checked against a named PCB STEP revision.
steps.guidelines: Review internal geometry against the current board layout with both revision numbers stated. Confirm standoff positions match mounting holes, that bosses and ribs do not collide with components, and that keep-outs given to hardware are reflected in the model. The failure mode is revision drift — each side internally consistent, working from different revisions, discovered at fit check.

steps.exitTrigger: External geometry finalised and fully dimensioned
steps.entryQuestion: Are all external dimensions final and tolerance-analysed?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the tolerance stack-up been analysed on every critical dimension chain?
steps.whatToDo: Create the tolerance stack-up: every contributing dimension, its tolerance, and the worst-case and RSS result at each critical interface.
steps.guidelines: Fix external geometry and dimension it fully. Run the tolerance stack-up on every critical chain — board to boss to aperture, lid to base at the seal, button to actuator. Stack-up analysis is the difference between a design that fits at nominal and one that fits across a production distribution, and it is the step most often skipped under schedule pressure with predictable consequences at first article.

steps.exitTrigger: Internal geometry complete and verified against the board
steps.entryQuestion: Is every internal feature — bosses, ribs, guides, seals, cable routes — defined?
steps.exitQuestion: Is there clearance for assembly access, cable routing and service?
steps.whatToDo: Record the internal design: bosses, ribs, standoffs, light pipes, cable routes and service access.
steps.guidelines: Complete internal features: mounting bosses with correct proportions, ribs for stiffness, cable routes and retention, sealing grooves, light pipes, button actuators. Check assembly access — a design that fits statically but cannot be assembled by hand in the intended sequence is still a failure, and this is only visible by walking the assembly order mentally or in the model.

steps.entryTrigger: Internal geometry complete and PCB STEP received from hardware
steps.exitTrigger: Full assembly built with the board in place and interference checked
steps.entryQuestion: Is the STEP file at the current board revision?
steps.exitQuestion: Are there zero interferences and adequate clearance at worst-case tolerance?
steps.whatToDo: Create the fit report and record the CAD-level interference check against the PCB STEP file, at tolerance extremes rather than nominal.
steps.guidelines: Import the released PCB STEP and build the full assembly. Run interference detection and check clearances against the tolerance stack-up rather than nominal. Verify connector alignment with apertures, indicator alignment with light pipes, and that tall components clear the lid. State the board revision this assembly was checked against — that number is what makes the check meaningful later.

steps.exitTrigger: Renders produced and reviewed internally
steps.entryQuestion: Do the renders represent the actual model rather than an idealised version?
steps.exitQuestion: Do the renders show the design as it will actually be manufactured, including parting lines?
steps.whatToDo: Record the render review: finish, texture, parting line visibility, and every cosmetic decision that will be judged on the moulded part.
steps.guidelines: Render from the actual CAD, showing parting lines, gate positions and realistic surface finish. Renders that hide these features create client expectations that the moulded part cannot meet, and the gap is discovered when the first article arrives. Show the product from the angles a user will actually see it.

steps.exitTrigger: Joint render review complete
steps.entryQuestion: Has hardware confirmed the rendered configuration matches the current design?
steps.exitQuestion: Do indicator positions, connector openings and markings match the board and the datasheet?
steps.whatToDo: Add the render review with hardware for anything that affects LEDs, displays, antennas or venting.
steps.guidelines: Check the renders against the hardware design: indicator positions, connector apertures, labelling and marking positions. This is a cheap cross-check that catches mismatches which would otherwise reach the client as an approved image and become a commitment.

steps.exitTrigger: Design approval received in writing
steps.entryQuestion: Has the client seen the design and understood what they are approving?
steps.exitQuestion: Is it clear to the client that this approves form and finish, not yet verified fit?
steps.whatToDo: Record the design approval: who approved, against which CAD revision, and on what date.
