steps.guidelines: Obtain approval in writing with the scope of the approval stated: this approves form, finish and layout, not verified fit or moulded surface quality. Clients frequently believe an approved render is a commitment to an exact appearance, and moulded parts differ from renders in ways worth stating now — gate marks, sink, parting lines, texture variation.

steps.exitTrigger: Physical prototype printed and inspected
steps.entryQuestion: Is the print process appropriate for what needs to be verified?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the print represent the geometry accurately enough for the check being made?
steps.whatToDo: Record the 3D print: material, machine, layer height and the tolerance actually achieved. A printed part is not a moulded part and the differences matter.
steps.guidelines: Select the process for the purpose: SLA for surface and appearance, SLS or FDM for functional fit and strength. Know the tolerance the process holds — a fit check on a part printed with looser tolerance than the moulded part will hold tells you less than it appears to. Print the mating parts together so the assembly can be checked, not just the individual geometry.

steps.entryTrigger: Physical prototype available and a board to fit it
steps.exitTrigger: Fit and assembly verified physically with findings recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Is a representative board available to check against?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the board fit, do connectors align, and can it be assembled in the intended sequence?
steps.whatToDo: Record the physical fit check: what fitted, what did not, and by how much. Measured, not observed.
steps.guidelines: Assemble the actual board into the printed enclosure in the intended production sequence. Check board fit, standoff alignment, connector to aperture alignment, cable routing, closure and any fasteners. Record every finding with a photograph. This is the first physical truth about the mechanical design and it routinely surfaces issues no amount of CAD review would have found.

steps.exitTrigger: First design iteration reviewed with changes agreed
steps.entryQuestion: Are all findings from the physical check captured with a disposition?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every finding either designed out or accepted with rationale?
steps.whatToDo: Record the design 1 review against the fit findings, criterion by criterion.
steps.guidelines: Review the fit check findings and decide the disposition for each: design change, tolerance adjustment, or accept with rationale. Group the changes into one coherent iteration rather than making them piecemeal — a sequence of individual edits produces a model whose current state nobody is confident about, and it undermines the second fit check.

steps.exitTrigger: CAD updated with all agreed changes and revision incremented
steps.entryQuestion: Are all agreed changes scoped and their knock-on effects understood?
steps.exitQuestion: Have the changes been checked for knock-on effects on fit, tolerance and moulding?
steps.whatToDo: Revise the CAD against the findings and bump the revision. Record what changed and why.
steps.guidelines: Apply the agreed changes and re-check for knock-on effects — moving a boss can violate wall thickness, changing a wall can alter the stack-up, deepening a rib can create a sink mark on a visible surface. Increment the revision and notify hardware if anything affects the board interface, because they are designing against the previous revision until told otherwise.

steps.exitTrigger: Second-iteration renders produced and reviewed
steps.entryQuestion: Do the updated renders reflect all changes made?
steps.exitQuestion: Are all changes from the first iteration visible and correct in the renders?
steps.whatToDo: Record the second render review against the revised CAD.
steps.guidelines: Re-render from the updated model and review against the change list to confirm each change is present and correct. This catches changes that were agreed but not actually applied — a common gap when several edits are made across a model in one sitting.

steps.exitTrigger: Joint second-iteration review complete
steps.entryQuestion: Has hardware confirmed the changes do not affect the board interface?
steps.exitQuestion: Do any of the changes require a corresponding hardware change?
steps.whatToDo: Add the second render review with hardware.
steps.guidelines: Confirm with hardware that the second iteration has not altered anything they depend on — mounting positions, connector apertures, internal height, thermal path. Where it has, agree the corresponding hardware change now, while both tracks are still in design and the change is cheap on both sides.

steps.exitTrigger: Second design approval received in writing
steps.entryQuestion: Has the client reviewed the changes made since the first approval?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the client approving the current revision, and is that revision number recorded?
steps.whatToDo: Record the iteration-2 design approval against the named CAD revision.
steps.guidelines: Obtain approval on the second iteration with the revision number stated explicitly in the approval. Approvals that do not name a revision are the reason disputes about what was approved cannot be settled. Confirm the client has seen what changed since the first approval rather than assuming they have noticed.

steps.exitTrigger: Second-iteration prototype printed
steps.entryQuestion: Is a second print justified by the extent of the changes?
steps.exitQuestion: Does this print incorporate every change from the first iteration?
steps.whatToDo: Record the second print and what it was checking that the first one could not.
steps.guidelines: Print the revised design to verify the changes worked. Confirm the print is from the current revision — printing a superseded file produces a fit check that validates nothing and consumes the schedule anyway. Where changes were minor and localised, printing only the affected part may be sufficient and faster.

steps.exitTrigger: Second fit check complete with all previous findings verified closed
steps.entryQuestion: Are the first-iteration findings the specific focus of this check?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every first-iteration finding demonstrably resolved, with no new issues introduced?
steps.whatToDo: Record the iteration-2 fit check with measurements, and confirm the earlier findings are actually closed.
steps.guidelines: Re-run the full assembly check with particular attention to the first-iteration findings. Verify each is resolved and check that no new issue was introduced by the changes. Record with photographs. If findings remain open after this iteration, decide deliberately whether to iterate again or accept — but decide, rather than proceeding while carrying an unresolved fit issue into tooling.

steps.step: Final Enclosure Design Review and Release
steps.entryTrigger: Fit checks complete and all findings closed
steps.exitTrigger: Enclosure design released as a frozen baseline
steps.entryQuestion: Are all findings closed and is the design manufacturable as drawn?
steps.exitQuestion: Have manufacturability, tolerance and fit all been signed off?
steps.whatToDo: Release the final enclosure design. Record the revision and the approver — everything downstream cites this.
steps.guidelines: Final review covering manufacturability, tolerance stack-up, fit verification and cosmetic requirements. Release as a frozen, versioned baseline — tooling will be quoted and cut against this and changes after tool cut are measured in weeks and tooling cost. Confirm hardware is working to the matching board revision.

steps.exitTrigger: Full assembly STEP released
steps.entryQuestion: Is the assembly at the released revisions of both enclosure and board?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the assembly file state both the enclosure and PCB revisions it contains?
steps.whatToDo: Release the STEP file that includes the PCB, and log its revision against the PCB revision it contains.
steps.guidelines: Export the full assembly including the board and state both revision numbers in the file name and the release note. This file is the reference for anyone needing to understand the complete product geometry — tooling vendors, assembly planners, service documentation — and its value depends on knowing exactly which revisions it represents.

steps.exitTrigger: Individual enclosure part STEP files released
steps.entryQuestion: Are the individual part files clean and at the released revision?
steps.exitQuestion: Is there a separate file per moulded part, correctly named?
steps.whatToDo: Release the enclosure-only STEP file at a named revision.
steps.guidelines: Export each moulded part as its own STEP for the tooling vendor. Name each per the convention with its revision. Verify each exports cleanly without geometry errors — a STEP with broken geometry will be repaired by the toolmaker using their own judgement, and their judgement about your parting line is not your judgement.

steps.exitTrigger: STL files released for prototyping and reference
steps.entryQuestion: Is the mesh resolution appropriate for the intended use?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the mesh resolution adequate on curved surfaces?
steps.whatToDo: Release the STL files, noting they are for printing and are not the manufacturing master.
steps.guidelines: Export STL at a resolution that preserves curved surfaces — a coarse mesh produces visible faceting on a printed part and misrepresents the design in review. Keep STL for prototyping and visualisation only; STEP is the file of record for manufacturing because STL carries no true geometry.

steps.exitTrigger: 2D manufacturing drawings released
steps.entryQuestion: Are all critical dimensions, tolerances and finish requirements specified?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every critical dimension carry a tolerance and every surface a finish specification?
steps.whatToDo: Create the 2D drawing pack: every dimension, tolerance, datum, material, finish and critical-to-function feature marked.
steps.guidelines: Produce drawings with critical dimensions, tolerances, GD&T where it matters, material specification, surface finish, texture, and colour reference. The drawing is the contractual definition of the part — where it and the model disagree, the drawing governs, so it must be complete. Include inspection dimensions so incoming quality has something specific to measure.

steps.exitTrigger: Mechanical BOM reviewed for completeness
steps.entryQuestion: Is every mechanical part, fastener and consumable listed?
steps.exitQuestion: Are fasteners, seals, adhesives, labels and light pipes all present?
steps.whatToDo: Check the mechanical BOM: every part, quantity, material, finish, supplier and the drawing it refers to.
steps.guidelines: Review the BOM for the parts that are routinely omitted: fasteners, washers, seals, gaskets, adhesives, tapes, light pipes, labels, thermal pads. These are individually trivial and collectively the reason a build stops. Specify each with a real part number and source rather than a description.

steps.step: Mechanical BoM Review with HW & FW
steps.exitTrigger: Cross-domain BOM review complete
steps.entryQuestion: Have hardware and firmware confirmed nothing they depend on is missing?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the combined BOM cover every part needed to build a complete unit?
steps.whatToDo: Add the joint mechanical BOM review with hardware and firmware — the combined BOM must build one complete unit with nothing missing.
steps.guidelines: Convergence point across all three tracks. Reconcile mechanical, electronics and any firmware-related items — programming adapters, test jigs, serial number labels — so that the combined BOM builds a complete unit. Items that fall between two BOMs are the ones nobody orders, and they are found on the assembly line.

steps.exitTrigger: Mechanical BOM released
steps.entryQuestion: Are all part numbers, quantities and sources final?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every line sourced with a real part number and a confirmed lead time?
steps.whatToDo: Release the mechanical BOM at a named revision.
steps.guidelines: Release with part numbers, quantities, sources and lead times. Flag long-lead items, particularly anything tooled or custom-moulded, and feed them into the procurement plan immediately. Reconcile into the multilevel BOM so there is a single structure procurement orders against.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly drawing produced showing sequence and fastening
steps.entryQuestion: Is the assembly sequence defined and physically verified?
steps.exitQuestion: Can an operator assemble the product correctly from this drawing alone?
steps.whatToDo: Create the assembly drawing: sequence, orientation, fastener torque and every operation the assembler must not guess.
steps.guidelines: Show the assembly sequence with an exploded view, fastener call-outs with torque where it matters, cable routing, and any adhesive or sealing step with its cure requirement. The drawing must be sufficient on its own for an operator who has not seen the product before, because that is the situation it will be used in.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly documentation reviewed against the actual build
steps.entryQuestion: Do the assembly documents cover the full build including test and packing?
steps.exitQuestion: Has someone assembled a unit following only these documents?
steps.whatToDo: Check the product assembly documents: complete, current revision, and buildable by someone who has never seen the product.
steps.guidelines: Test the documentation by having someone build a unit from it without assistance. Every question they ask is a gap in the document. Check that the sequence includes programming, testing, labelling and packing rather than stopping at mechanical assembly — the line needs the whole flow, not the part that mechanical owns.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly documentation released to production
steps.entryQuestion: Are all documents at consistent revisions?
steps.exitQuestion: Do the assembly documents reference the correct BOM and drawing revisions?
steps.whatToDo: Release the product assembly documents at a named revision.
steps.guidelines: Release the complete set at consistent revisions and confirm cross-references to BOM and drawings resolve correctly. Provide to the EMS as part of the production handover package. Documentation released at mismatched revisions is worse than incomplete documentation because it is trusted.

steps.exitTrigger: Enclosure DFMA review complete with findings addressed
steps.entryQuestion: Has the design been assessed for both manufacturability and assembly at volume?
steps.exitQuestion: Are part count, assembly time and tooling complexity all justified?
steps.whatToDo: Work the DFM sheet: wall thickness variation, draft, undercuts, sink risk, warpage and gate location. Every finding is actioned or waived before tooling.
steps.guidelines: Assess moulding feasibility — draft, wall uniformity, gate location, ejection, cycle time — and assembly efficiency: part count, fastener count, orientation changes required, whether parts can be assembled in one direction. Every part removed and every fastener eliminated compounds across the production volume. Involve the toolmaker; their process knowledge finds things a designer will not.

steps.step: Enclosure DFM review against the moulder's capability
steps.entryTrigger: Enclosure DFMA review complete and the moulder identified
steps.exitTrigger: Draft angles, wall sections, rib ratios, boss geometry and gate positions checked against the named moulder's capability sheet
steps.entryQuestion: Has the moulder who will actually cut the tool seen this geometry?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the moulder confirmed in writing that the part is mouldable as drawn, at the stated cycle time and finish?
steps.whatToDo: Add the moulder's own comments to the sheet and their written confirmation that the part is mouldable as drawn, at the stated cycle time and finish.
steps.guidelines: DFMA asks whether the design is sensible; this asks whether this moulder can cut this tool. Send the CAD to the named moulder and get their comments on draft, wall thickness variation, rib-to-wall ratio, boss design, gate and ejector positions, and the finish they can hold. Tool changes after steel is cut are paid for in weeks, not rupees.

steps.exitTrigger: Required iterations complete and re-verified
steps.entryQuestion: Which findings justify a design iteration before tooling is committed?
steps.exitQuestion: Have all changes been re-checked for fit, tolerance and cross-track impact?
steps.whatToDo: Apply the required iterations, bump the revision, and re-verify the findings that triggered them.
steps.guidelines: Iterate on findings that materially affect cost, quality or feasibility, and accept the rest with rationale recorded. Re-verify fit, tolerance and moulding after each change. Iterating now costs days; the same change after tool cut costs weeks and tooling modification, which is why the DFMA review sits before tooling commitment rather than after.

steps.exitTrigger: Enclosure section of the Audit Checklist populated with a link, a status, a date and an updater on every Required row
steps.entryQuestion: Is every enclosure artefact named to convention and filed at its path in the sitemap?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every Required row in this section carry all four cells — Status, Link, Last updated and Updated by?
steps.whatToDo: Update the enclosure section: concept, CAD, 2D drawings, manufacturing drawings, mechanical BOM and the vendor SAR.
steps.guidelines: Paste the artefact filename into Links, set Status from the dropdown, stamp the date and record who updated it. Cover concept, CAD, 2D drawings, manufacturing drawings, mechanical BOM and the selected vendor SAR. A row with a link but no status is an artefact nobody has accepted, and a status with no link is a claim with no evidence behind it.

steps.entryTrigger: All enclosure artefacts released and DFMA closed
steps.exitTrigger: Enclosure release checklist closed and the track's outputs complete
steps.entryQuestion: Is every enclosure output present, versioned and stored correctly?
steps.exitQuestion: Are CAD, drawings, BOM, assembly documents and artwork all present at consistent revisions?
steps.whatToDo: Close the enclosure section: every Required row complete with all four cells.
steps.guidelines: Close out the enclosure output pack: CAD with and without PCB, 2D drawings, manufacturing drawings, assembly drawings, mechanical BOM, material and colour and process documentation, logo and marking artwork, vendor SAR, and production process flowchart. Verify consistent revisions and correct storage. This closure is the enclosure track's exit into the merged Prototype stage.

steps.exitTrigger: Material test plan approved
steps.entryQuestion: Are the material grade, supplier and process confirmed?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the plan cover the properties the application actually depends on?
steps.whatToDo: Create the material test plan: which properties are being proven, to which standard, on how many samples.
steps.guidelines: Plan tests for the properties this product genuinely relies on — tensile and impact strength, UV resistance where it sits outdoors, flammability rating, chemical resistance where it is cleaned. Reference the standard for each. Testing everything is wasteful; testing the wrong three things is worse.

steps.exitTrigger: Material test reports received and reviewed
steps.entryQuestion: Is the sample from the same batch and process as production intent?
steps.exitQuestion: Do results meet the specification, including the flammability rating claimed?
steps.whatToDo: Record the material results with measured values against the datasheet claim, and note any deviation.
steps.guidelines: Test samples from the intended production process, not from a 3D print, because material behaviour is a function of process as much as polymer. Verify the flammability rating in particular — it is the property most often assumed from a datasheet and least often confirmed, and it is the one a certification body will ask to see.

steps.exitTrigger: Enclosure test plan approved covering all applicable families
steps.entryQuestion: Which mechanical and environmental families apply to this product?
steps.exitQuestion: Is each test tied to a standard and an acceptance criterion?
steps.whatToDo: Create the enclosure test plan covering fit, drop, ingress, vibration, mechanism life and cosmetics.
steps.guidelines: Scope the families that apply — drop, IP, vibration, mechanism life, cosmetic — and mark the ones that do not, with a reason. Tie each to its standard and acceptance criterion. Marking a family not-applicable is a legitimate decision; leaving it undecided is not.

steps.step: Fit and Interference Verification with Assembled PCB
steps.entryTrigger: Enclosure parts and assembled PCB both available
steps.exitTrigger: Fit verified at worst-case tolerance with findings recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Is the PCB at the revision the enclosure was designed around?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the assembly close cleanly with the tolerance stack applied?
steps.whatToDo: Record the fit and interference verification with the assembled PCB installed, measured at the critical interfaces.
steps.guidelines: Assemble a real board into a real enclosure and check clearance at worst-case tolerance rather than nominal, including connector access, standoff alignment and cable routing. Nominal always fits. The stack-up is what determines whether the hundredth unit does.

steps.exitTrigger: Drop test executed and results photographed
steps.entryQuestion: Is the drop height and orientation set from the standard or the use case?
steps.exitQuestion: Did the unit remain functional and the enclosure remain intact?
steps.whatToDo: Record the drop test: orientation, height, surface, unit count and the damage observed on each.
steps.guidelines: Drop from the agreed height on faces, edges and corners, with the unit fully assembled and populated so mass distribution is real. Photograph before and after every drop and functionally retest. A drop test with no photographic record cannot support a design change argument later.

steps.exitTrigger: IP verification executed and result recorded against the claimed rating
steps.entryQuestion: Is the sealing method final, including gaskets and cable entries?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the unit meet the exact rating being claimed on the datasheet?
steps.whatToDo: Record the IP verification per IEC 60529: rating claimed, method used, duration and the ingress observed.
steps.guidelines: Verify against the specific rating claimed, following IEC 60529 for both the dust and water digits, with all cable entries and any user-accessible flap in their normal state. Open the unit afterwards and inspect for ingress. A rating printed on a datasheet and never verified is a warranty liability with a number on it.

steps.exitTrigger: Vibration and shock profiles executed and results recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Does the profile reflect transport, installation or in-use vibration?
steps.exitQuestion: Did any fastener loosen, solder joint crack or connector unseat?
steps.whatToDo: Record vibration and shock: profile, axes, duration and every loosening or fracture found afterwards.
steps.guidelines: Run the profile that matches how the product actually travels and operates, then inspect fasteners, solder joints and connectors afterwards rather than relying on a functional pass. Loosening shows up before failure does, and catching it here is the difference between a design change and a field recall.

steps.exitTrigger: Life cycling completed to the agreed count with condition recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Is the cycle count target agreed with the client?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the mechanism still meet its force and travel specification at end of life?
steps.whatToDo: Record mechanism life cycling: cycles run, force at start and end, and the failure mode when it eventually fails.
steps.guidelines: Cycle to the agreed count — typically 10,000 to 100,000 depending on use — and measure actuation force and travel at the start and the end, not only at the end. Degradation curves tell you where the real life limit is; a single end-point measurement only tells you it survived the number you chose.

steps.step: Cosmetic Inspection and First Article Inspection
steps.entryTrigger: Parts received from the tool or process
steps.exitTrigger: Cosmetic and dimensional inspection completed and signed
steps.entryQuestion: Is the cosmetic standard agreed and documented with a reference sample?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every dimension match the drawing within tolerance?
steps.whatToDo: Record the cosmetic and first-article inspection against the drawing: every dimension checked, and every cosmetic defect classified.
steps.guidelines: Inspect every dimension on the drawing against the first article and assess cosmetics against an agreed reference sample rather than personal judgement. Sign it. Cosmetic disputes with a vendor are unwinnable without a reference sample agreed in advance, and dimensional disputes are unwinnable without an FAI.

steps.step: Enclosure Defect Log and Root Cause Analysis
steps.exitTrigger: Every defect closed with root cause and disposition
steps.entryQuestion: Is each defect logged against the part revision and the process used?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every defect have a root cause and a verified corrective action?
steps.whatToDo: Log every enclosure defect against the part revision and the process used, with root cause and disposition.
steps.guidelines: Log defects against part revision and manufacturing process, and separate design causes from process causes — they route to different owners and different fixes. Verify each corrective action by retest. Feed the outcome into the DFM review before the tool is cut, which is the last point at which a design cause is cheap to fix.

steps.exitTrigger: Enclosure test reports issued for every applicable test family
steps.entryQuestion: Are the environmental and mechanical test parameters available to test against?
steps.exitQuestion: Are IP rating, drop, vibration and mechanism life results all recorded?
steps.whatToDo: Assemble the enclosure test report linking plan, procedure and results for every test.
steps.guidelines: Issue the mechanical and environmental reports: material test results, drop, IP verification per IEC 60529, vibration and shock, button and mechanism life cycling, cosmetic inspection and first article inspection. Photograph failures. A drop test with no photographic record cannot support a design change argument later.

steps.step: Audit Checklist update — Enclosure test evidence
steps.exitTrigger: Enclosure test rows in the Audit Checklist carry measured evidence and an approval status
steps.entryQuestion: Are all enclosure test reports complete with measured values rather than pass marks?
steps.exitQuestion: Is each test row linked to its parameter document, procedure document and report?
steps.whatToDo: Update the enclosure test rows with measured evidence and links.
steps.guidelines: Link all three artefacts per test family — parameters, procedure and report — not just the report. The checklist is the only place the three are visibly tied together, and a report whose parameters cannot be located cannot be defended when a result is later questioned.

steps.entryTrigger: All three design tracks closed and test reports issued
steps.exitTrigger: Prototype checklist complete and build authorised
steps.entryQuestion: Are all eight prototype checklist inputs present and at consistent revisions?
steps.exitQuestion: Do the multilevel BOM, PCB files, assembly checklist, code upload document, pick and place, stackup document, wiring document and assembly drawings all reconcile?
steps.whatToDo: Create the EVT build record and confirm all three tracks reconcile at one revision before anything is ordered.
steps.guidelines: This is the merge point where the hardware, firmware and enclosure tracks converge into one build. Verify all eight inputs are present and at consistent revisions: multilevel BOM, PCB files, assembly checklist, code upload document, pick and place, PCB stackup document, PCB wiring document and assembly drawings. A revision mismatch between any two of these produces a build that is wrong in a way nobody notices until test.

steps.exitTrigger: Budget approved and payment route confirmed
steps.entryQuestion: Is the prototype build cost within the sanctioned budget?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the approval recorded with the project ID and the expected spend by category?
steps.whatToDo: Update the budget with the actual prototype cost and record the approval against it.
steps.guidelines: Raise the prototype budget with the spend broken down by category — BOM, PCB, assembly, logistics, enclosures — so actuals can be tracked against plan afterwards. Route through the approval group with the project ID attached. Approval sought after committing the order is not approval, and it is the pattern that produces unreconcilable project costs.

steps.exitTrigger: All BOM parts ordered with delivery dates confirmed
steps.entryQuestion: Are all parts available within the build schedule, with alternates for long-lead items?
steps.exitQuestion: Will every part arrive before assembly is scheduled to start?
steps.whatToDo: Update the consolidated BOM with what was actually ordered: supplier, quantity, price, lead time and expected date per line.
steps.guidelines: Order against the released multilevel BOM through the channel priority: Digikey, then Robu, then Mouser. Confirm delivery dates in writing and track them against the assembly date — one late part holds the entire build, so the critical path is the longest lead time, not the average. Where a part is unavailable, use the identified alternate rather than substituting on judgement; a substitution made at the desk becomes a board that does not match its documentation.

steps.entryTrigger: Hardware, firmware and enclosure DFx closed on their own tracks
steps.exitTrigger: One product-level DFx view issued covering all three tracks, every open waiver and every cross-track dependency
steps.entryQuestion: Have the three tracks been looked at together, or only separately?
steps.exitQuestion: Does any finding close on one track only because another track quietly absorbed the problem?
steps.whatToDo: Create the consolidation report and put the three tracks' DFx registers side by side. Look for the findings that moved to another track rather than closed.
steps.guidelines: Three tracks each closing their own DFx is not the same as the product being manufacturable. Put the three registers side by side and look for the findings that moved rather than closed — a hardware clearance solved by a moulded rib, a test point solved by a firmware readback, a thermal problem solved by an enclosure vent. Each of those is now a dependency between two tracks and it needs to be visible to whoever changes either one.

steps.entryTrigger: Product-level DFx consolidation issued and gates G0 to G2 released
steps.exitTrigger: Written authorisation to place fabrication and assembly orders, naming the exact revision of every released file
steps.entryQuestion: Are all DFx gates up to G2 released, and is every waiver Accepted rather than Draft?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the authorisation name the exact revision of every file going to the fabricator and to the EMS?
steps.whatToDo: Create the authorisation and name the exact revision of every file going to the fabricator and the EMS. This is the only record of what they were actually given.
steps.guidelines: This is the single point at which money is committed to a physical build. Name every file and its revision — Gerber or ODB++, drill, netlist, stencil, pick-and-place, BOM, assembly drawing, panel drawing. When a build later goes wrong, the first question is which revision the supplier actually received, and this document is the only place that is answerable.

steps.entryTrigger: Gerber and panel files released and budget approved
steps.exitTrigger: PCB order placed with fabrication files and stackup confirmed
steps.entryQuestion: Has the fabricator confirmed they can build this stackup to the stated impedance?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the fabricator raised any DFM query, and has it been answered by engineering rather than assumed?
steps.whatToDo: Create the PCB specification sheet for the fabricator: stack-up, material, finish, tolerance, IPC class and every special requirement.
steps.guidelines: Order against the released Gerber, drill, IPC-356 and panel files with the stackup specification attached. Fabricator DFM queries come back to engineering for a decision — a query answered by procurement to save time is a design change made by someone without the context to make it. Confirm impedance control and electrical test are included in the order.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly vendor selected and briefed
steps.entryQuestion: Does the assembler have the capability for this board's component set and process?
steps.exitQuestion: Can they handle the finest pitch, the smallest passive and any special process this board needs?
steps.whatToDo: Create the EMS audit checklist and assess the candidate assembly vendor against it — capability, capacity, quality system and traceability.
steps.guidelines: Select against actual capability: finest pitch, smallest passive size, BGA and X-ray availability, AOI, conformal coating, and any hand-assembly steps. Brief them with the full documentation package and confirm they can execute the assembly instruction as written. Establish the pick and place rotation convention explicitly before files are sent.

steps.entryTrigger: Parts and boards arriving from suppliers
steps.exitTrigger: All incoming goods received and checked against the checklist
steps.entryQuestion: Is there a defined checklist against which incoming goods are verified?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every received item match its order in part number, quantity and revision?
steps.whatToDo: Create the pre-assembly QC record and check incoming material against the BOM: part number, quantity, date code, MSL and packaging condition.
steps.guidelines: Check every delivery against the order: part number, manufacturer, quantity, date code, packaging condition and moisture barrier integrity. Check the board revision on the silkscreen against what was ordered. Log receipt against the project. Parts accepted without checking become defects attributed to the design at test, and the true cause is never found.

steps.exitTrigger: Incoming quality inspection complete and report issued
steps.entryQuestion: Are the inspection criteria defined for each incoming item class?
steps.exitQuestion: Have bare boards been electrically tested and dimensionally checked before assembly?
steps.whatToDo: Record the IQC result per line: accepted, rejected, or accepted with deviation and its reason.
steps.guidelines: Inspect incoming goods to defined criteria: bare board electrical test results and dimensional check, component authenticity and date code, moisture sensitivity handling, mechanical part dimensions against the drawing. Reject and document rather than accepting marginal material — a marginal bare board becomes an assembled board that fails, and by then the cost is the whole assembly.

steps.entryTrigger: IQC passed and all materials available
steps.exitTrigger: Assembly checklist confirmed complete by the EMS before build starts
steps.entryQuestion: Does the assembler hold the complete documentation set at consistent revisions?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the EMS confirmed every listed item is present and executable?
steps.whatToDo: Create the assembly QC record and confirm the EMS holds the complete documentation set before the build starts.
steps.guidelines: Confirm the EMS holds every item on the list and has raised any gap before the line starts. The list covers the full documentation set, the materials, the stencil, the profile and the test arrangement. A build that starts with a missing item stops midway, and restarting a partially built panel is more expensive than the delay would have been.

steps.exitTrigger: Complete package cross-checked and dispatched to the assembler
steps.entryQuestion: Has every file and material been verified one final time against the release revisions?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every item in the dispatched package at the same released revision?
steps.whatToDo: Check the pack being sent against the released revision list, line by line. This is the last point before someone builds to the wrong file.
steps.guidelines: Final verification before dispatch: every file at its released revision, every material present, quantities correct. This is the last point at which a mismatch costs minutes rather than a build. Record what was sent and when, so that if a question arises later there is no ambiguity about which revision the assembler received.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembled boards received and inspected
steps.entryQuestion: Have the boards passed AOI and any required X-ray inspection?
steps.exitQuestion: Do the boards match the assembly drawing, including do-not-populate items?
steps.whatToDo: Record the post-assembly result: AOI, X-ray, first pass yield and the dominant defect mode.
steps.guidelines: Receive and inspect against the assembly drawing: correct parts, correct orientation, do-not-populate items genuinely unpopulated, solder quality, no bridging or tombstoning. Review the AOI and X-ray results rather than accepting a pass summary. Photograph the first article top and bottom for the record — that photograph becomes the reference for every subsequent build.

steps.entryTrigger: Assembled boards available and firmware released
steps.exitTrigger: Firmware flashed and boards verified operational
steps.entryQuestion: Is the correct firmware version identified and available to the line?
steps.exitQuestion: Does each board report the expected git hash at boot?
steps.whatToDo: Record the flashing run: firmware version, hash, unit count, failures and the recovery route used.
steps.guidelines: Flash production test firmware first, run the board-level functional test, then load the application firmware. Confirm each board reports the expected git hash at boot — that check catches a wrong or partial image immediately rather than at product test. Record results per board so a unit that behaves oddly later can be traced to what was actually loaded onto it.

steps.exitTrigger: Reliability testing complete and report issued
steps.entryQuestion: Are the reliability parameters and the test procedure both defined?
steps.exitQuestion: Do results meet the reliability and MTBF parameters set at feasibility?
steps.whatToDo: Record the prototype reliability run with measured values, duration and every failure.
steps.guidelines: Run reliability testing against the parameters set at feasibility: burn-in for 24 to 72 hours, thermal cycling, and where scoped, HALT to find design margins. Record measured values and any drift over the test. A reliability report that records only pass or fail gives no view of margin, and margin is the whole point of the exercise.

steps.exitTrigger: Functional testing complete and report issued
steps.entryQuestion: Are the board-level and product-level functional test parameters available?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the product behave exactly as the logic sheet specifies in every state?
steps.whatToDo: Record the prototype functional results per unit serial, with measured values against the parameter limits.
steps.guidelines: Test against the board-level and product-level functional parameters, walking the logic sheet state by state including fault and recovery paths. Record measured values against each parameter. Where behaviour differs from the logic sheet, the discrepancy is logged as an issue — deciding on the spot which one is correct is how undocumented behaviour enters a product.

steps.exitTrigger: UAT complete and client sign-off obtained
steps.entryQuestion: Has the client defined what they will test and what constitutes acceptance?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the client tested against agreed criteria and signed the result?
steps.whatToDo: Create the UAT record: cases run with the client, their result, and what the client asked for that is not in the spec.
steps.guidelines: Run UAT against criteria agreed with the client in advance, not against criteria they form while testing. Support the session but let them operate the product. Record every observation including the ones that are not defects — usability observations become change requests later and are cheaper to discuss now. Obtain written sign-off on the tested revision.

steps.exitTrigger: All prototype issues logged, dispositioned and closed or carried forward
steps.entryQuestion: Is there a single tracker capturing every issue from this build?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every issue have a root cause, a disposition and an owner?
steps.whatToDo: Create the issue tracker and log every prototype issue with severity, owner, root cause and the fix's target revision.
steps.guidelines: Log every issue from the build in one place per build with severity, root cause, disposition and owner. Issues held in individual engineers' heads or in chat threads do not get closed and recur in the pilot build. Each issue is either fixed in this iteration, deferred with rationale, or accepted — and deferred issues carry into the pilot checklist explicitly.

steps.exitTrigger: Field trial complete with observations recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Is the deployment environment and trial duration agreed with the client?
steps.exitQuestion: Did the product behave in the field as it did on the bench, and if not, why not?
steps.whatToDo: Record the field trial: site, duration, unit count, conditions and every failure mode that in-house testing did not reproduce.
steps.guidelines: Deploy into the real environment for an agreed duration with a defined observation plan. The field surfaces what the bench cannot: real network conditions, real thermal environment, real user behaviour, real power quality. Instrument the units so behaviour can be observed remotely rather than relying on the user to report. Log every observation, including the ones without an obvious cause.

steps.exitTrigger: Iteration decision made and, if required, changes implemented and re-verified
steps.entryQuestion: Do the accumulated findings justify a design iteration before pilot?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the decision to iterate or proceed recorded with its rationale?
steps.whatToDo: Raise the required changes as ECN entries with impact, cost and the revision they land in.
steps.guidelines: Decide deliberately whether findings warrant a design iteration before committing to pilot volumes. Proceeding with known open issues is sometimes correct, but only as a recorded decision with the risk accepted by a named person. An issue carried forward silently becomes a pilot-quantity problem, and pilot quantities are where cost starts to matter.

steps.entryTrigger: All prototype testing complete and iteration decision made
steps.exitTrigger: DVT confirmation issued and client acknowledgement received
steps.entryQuestion: Are all test reports complete and is the design state unambiguous?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the client confirmed which revision they are approving to proceed to pilot?
steps.whatToDo: Create the DVT build record and confirm what was demonstrated to the client and what they agreed to in writing.
steps.guidelines: Confirm design validation completion in writing with the test reports attached and the exact revision named. State any accepted open issues explicitly rather than omitting them — an issue the client discovers later that was known internally is a trust problem, not a technical one. Obtain acknowledgement of which revision is approved for pilot.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly section populated with stencil, stack-up, pick-and-place, wiring and assembly instruction evidence
steps.entryQuestion: Are the assembly documents the ones actually used on the line?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every assembly row carry a link to the revision used for this build?
steps.whatToDo: Update the assembly rows with the revision of each document actually used for this build, not the latest on the drive.
steps.guidelines: Link the revision of each document that was genuinely used for this build, not the latest one on the drive. When a build yields badly, the first question is which document version the line ran to, and that is answerable only if it was recorded at the time.

steps.step: Audit Checklist gate review before pilot release
steps.entryTrigger: Prototype validated and all sections populated
steps.exitTrigger: Gate review passed — no Required row left unevidenced, and every exception formally accepted
steps.entryQuestion: Are all Required rows closed across hardware, firmware, enclosure, assembly and test?
steps.exitQuestion: For every row not closed, is there a named accepter and a written risk acceptance?
steps.whatToDo: Run the checklist as a gate. Every Required row closed, or waived with a named accepter and a written risk acceptance. Nothing else passes.
steps.guidelines: Run the checklist as a gate rather than a report. Every Required row is closed, waived with a named accepter, or the gate does not pass. This is the step that converts the checklist from a record into a control — if a project can reach pilot with rows still open and nobody named against them, the checklist is decorative.

steps.entryTrigger: All three design tracks merged at prototype
steps.exitTrigger: System integration test plan approved
steps.entryQuestion: Are all sub-system test reports closed before system testing begins?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the plan cover every interface between hardware, firmware and enclosure?
steps.whatToDo: Update the integration plan against the real build: what is actually integrated, in which order, and what proves the whole system works.
steps.guidelines: Plan the system test only once the three track-level test reports are closed, so system failures are genuinely system failures rather than sub-system defects surfacing late. Cover every interface and every end-to-end user path described in the LLD.

steps.exitTrigger: System integration executed with results recorded per interface
steps.entryQuestion: Is the unit assembled exactly as it will ship, including enclosure?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every end-to-end path behave as the LLD describes?
steps.whatToDo: Record the integration results, including every interface that failed at the boundary between two working subsystems.
steps.guidelines: Test the complete product as the customer will receive it — board in enclosure, production firmware, real connectivity. Sub-system passes do not sum to a system pass; thermal, EMI and mechanical effects only appear once everything is inside the same box.

steps.exitTrigger: Product-level functional test executed against the full feature list
steps.entryQuestion: Is every client-facing feature represented by a test case?
steps.exitQuestion: Is a result and evidence recorded against every feature?
steps.whatToDo: Record the product-level functional results in the user's terms, against the parameters agreed at feasibility.
steps.guidelines: Work from the client-facing feature list rather than the engineering one, testing what was sold and not only what was built. This is the last internal check before the product meets the client's expectations, and any gap between the two lists is far cheaper to find here.

steps.exitTrigger: In-house EMC pre-scan completed with margins recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Is the unit in its final enclosure with production cabling?
steps.exitQuestion: Where are the emission peaks and how much margin remains to the limit?
steps.whatToDo: Record the in-house EMC pre-scan: setup, frequencies, margins to the limit line, and the worst offender.
steps.guidelines: Scan in the final enclosure with production cabling, because both change the emission profile substantially. Record peak frequencies and margin rather than a pass or fail. Margin is what tells you whether the design will still pass after a component change or a second supplier.

steps.exitTrigger: Pre-compliance clean in-house across all applicable standards
steps.entryQuestion: Which standards apply on the chosen certification route?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the unit clean in-house before any lab booking is made?
steps.whatToDo: Record each pre-compliance iteration: what failed, what was changed, and the result after the change.
steps.guidelines: Iterate in-house until clean before booking an external lab. A failed lab visit costs the fee, the slot and typically four to six weeks of schedule, and it is almost always caused by something a pre-scan would have found.

steps.exitTrigger: Readiness review passed and lab booking confirmed
steps.entryQuestion: Is the full submission pack complete for the chosen route?
steps.exitQuestion: Has someone independent confirmed the unit and paperwork are lab-ready?
steps.whatToDo: Work the readiness review before booking the lab: sample condition, configuration, documentation and the test plan the lab will run.
steps.guidelines: Review the sample, the paperwork, the test setup and the submission pack together before the unit leaves the building. Labs reject submissions on documentation as often as on performance, and the rejection costs the same either way.

steps.exitTrigger: Lab testing completed and results received
steps.entryQuestion: Is the sample sealed, serialised and traceable to a build revision?
steps.exitQuestion: Did every applicable standard pass, and are failures root-caused?
steps.whatToDo: Record the external lab results and the exact configuration tested. Certification attaches to a configuration, not to a product name.
steps.guidelines: Send a serialised sample traceable to a specific build revision, and record which revision was certified. Certification attaches to a configuration, not to a product name — a later change can invalidate it, and you can only prove that if you recorded what was tested.

steps.exitTrigger: Certificates issued and entered in the register
steps.entryQuestion: Are all certificates received for the standards claimed?
steps.exitQuestion: Is each certificate linked to the exact build revision it covers?
steps.whatToDo: Add each certificate to the register with its number, scope, issuing body, expiry, and critically the build revision it covers.
steps.guidelines: Register every certificate against the build revision, issue date and expiry. This register is what allows a post-approval change to be assessed rather than guessed, and it is what a customer's compliance team will ask for first.

steps.exitTrigger: Stress limits characterised and operating margin documented
steps.entryQuestion: Is destructive testing budgeted and are sample units allocated?
steps.exitQuestion: Where does the product actually break, and how much margin does that leave?
steps.whatToDo: Record HALT and HASS: stress levels applied, the operating and destruct limits found, and the failure mode at each.
steps.guidelines: Push temperature, vibration and voltage beyond specification until the product fails, then record where and how. The purpose is not a pass — it is knowing the distance between the specification and the cliff edge, which is the only honest measure of design margin.

steps.exitTrigger: MTBF estimate produced and stated with its method
steps.entryQuestion: Is the component reliability data available for the final BOM?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the estimate state its method, assumptions and operating conditions?
steps.whatToDo: Create the MTBF estimate: method, standard, assumptions, part count and the resulting figure with its confidence.
steps.guidelines: Calculate from the final BOM, stating the standard used, the assumed operating conditions and the confidence level. An MTBF figure quoted without its assumptions is marketing rather than engineering, and it will be quoted back at you during a warranty dispute.

steps.step: Field Trial Plan and Unit Allocation
steps.exitTrigger: Field trial plan approved with units, sites and duration agreed
steps.entryQuestion: How many units, at which sites, for how long, and measuring what?
steps.exitQuestion: Is a data collection and failure reporting route agreed with the client?
steps.whatToDo: Create the field trial plan: sites, duration, unit allocation, data collected and the success criteria agreed in advance.
steps.guidelines: Agree the sample size, sites, duration and — most importantly — what is being measured and how it comes back. A field trial with no instrumented return path produces anecdotes, and anecdotes cannot be used to release a product.

steps.entryTrigger: Trial plan approved and units deployed
steps.exitTrigger: Trial completed and every finding root-caused
steps.entryQuestion: Are units instrumented and is data actually returning?
steps.exitQuestion: Has every field failure been root-caused rather than swapped out?
steps.whatToDo: Record trial execution and findings, including everything the users did that you did not anticipate.
steps.guidelines: Monitor for the agreed duration and root-cause every failure rather than replacing the unit and moving on. Field conditions surface what no chamber reproduces, and a replaced unit with no diagnosis is a defect that ships at volume.

steps.step: User Acceptance Testing and Client Sign-Off
steps.exitTrigger: UAT signed off by the client in writing
steps.entryQuestion: Is the client testing against the Testing Parameters agreed at feasibility?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the sign-off written, dated, and are open deviations formally accepted?
steps.whatToDo: Capture the client's UAT sign-off against a named build revision, with every accepted deviation listed.
steps.guidelines: Run UAT against the parameters agreed at feasibility, not against expectations formed since. Record the sign-off in writing with any deviations explicitly accepted as risks. A verbal acceptance is not a defence when the first volume shipment is disputed.

steps.step: Audit Checklist update — system test and compliance evidence
steps.entryTrigger: UAT signed off by the client
steps.exitTrigger: System, compliance and certification rows populated with evidence and certificate references
steps.entryQuestion: Are all compliance certificates received and linked to the build revision they cover?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every system-level row carry evidence, and is the certified revision recorded?
steps.whatToDo: Update the system and compliance rows: certificate number and the build revision each certificate covers.
steps.guidelines: Record the certificate number and, critically, the build revision each certificate covers. Certification attaches to a configuration and not to a product name. Without the revision recorded here, a later component change cannot be assessed for whether it invalidates the certificate.

steps.entryTrigger: DVT confirmed and client approval to proceed
steps.exitTrigger: Pilot order checklist complete and build authorised
steps.entryQuestion: Are all design changes from the prototype iteration incorporated and released?
steps.exitQuestion: Are all files at the post-iteration revision, and are quantities and dates agreed?
steps.whatToDo: Create the PVT build record: quantity, purpose, what the pilot is meant to prove, and the exit criteria.
steps.guidelines: Verify every file reflects the post-prototype iteration and that all deferred prototype issues have been dispositioned. Confirm pilot quantity, schedule and the acceptance criteria for the build. The purpose of pilot is to prove the process as much as the product, so plan to capture yield, cycle time and defect data from it.

steps.entryTrigger: Pilot checklist complete and budget approved
steps.exitTrigger: Orders placed with all vendors and delivery dates confirmed
steps.entryQuestion: Are vendor pricing and lead times confirmed at pilot volume?
steps.exitQuestion: Do pilot prices and lead times give a credible view of mass production economics?
steps.whatToDo: Raise the vendor purchase order with the agreed price, quantity, lead time and quality terms.
steps.guidelines: Negotiate at pilot volume while asking for indicative mass production pricing, since pilot pricing alone will mislead the business case. Confirm lead times at the higher volume — parts readily available in tens are sometimes allocated in thousands. Place orders against the released BOM with delivery dates tracked to the build schedule.

steps.exitTrigger: Full BOM verified complete with all deliveries tracked
steps.entryQuestion: Is every line of the multilevel BOM ordered and tracked?
steps.exitQuestion: Is any line unordered, unconfirmed, or arriving after the build date?
steps.whatToDo: Check the full BOM for the pilot: every line available at quantity, with lead time and second source confirmed.
steps.guidelines: Reconcile the multilevel BOM line by line against orders placed. Every line needs an order, a confirmed date and a tracking status. The lines that get missed are the small mechanical and consumable items — labels, screws, adhesives, packaging — and they stop a build as effectively as a missing MCU.

steps.entryTrigger: PCB files released at pilot revision
steps.exitTrigger: PCB fabrication package verified and ordered
steps.entryQuestion: Are the fabrication files, panel and stackup all at the correct revision?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the ordered board at the post-iteration revision?
steps.whatToDo: Check the PCB specification against what the fabricator quoted, and confirm the stack-up has not silently changed.
steps.guidelines: Verify the fabrication package is at the post-iteration revision and that any change made after prototype is present in the files being sent. Confirm panel, stackup, impedance control and electrical test are all specified. Ordering the prototype revision by mistake at pilot volume is an expensive and entirely avoidable error.

steps.entryTrigger: Enclosure design released at pilot revision
steps.exitTrigger: Enclosure package verified and ordered by the chosen route
steps.entryQuestion: Is the pilot enclosure route decided — printed, cast or tooled?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the pilot enclosure represent the moulded part closely enough to validate fit?
steps.whatToDo: Check the enclosure manufacturing drawings against the tool that will actually run, at the agreed finish.
steps.guidelines: Decide the pilot route: 3D printing, vacuum casting or soft tooling. Vacuum casting represents moulded parts better than printing and is usually the right choice at pilot quantities. Whichever route is chosen, understand where it differs from the production part in tolerance and finish, because those differences determine what the pilot can and cannot validate.

steps.exitTrigger: All pilot materials received and verified
steps.entryQuestion: Is every incoming delivery checked against its order?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every received item match its order in part number, quantity and revision?
steps.whatToDo: Create the pilot receiving record and check incoming material against the BOM, line by line.
steps.guidelines: Check every delivery against the order as at prototype, with more attention to quantity reconciliation since pilot volumes make shortfalls harder to spot and more disruptive. Verify board revision on the silkscreen. Log everything against the project so material consumption can be reconciled after the build.

steps.exitTrigger: Incoming quality inspection complete with sampling applied
steps.entryQuestion: Are inspection criteria and sampling plans defined for pilot volume?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the sampling plan statistically meaningful at this quantity?
steps.whatToDo: Record the pilot IQC result, including every deviation accepted and by whom.
steps.guidelines: Apply a defined sampling plan rather than inspecting every unit or inspecting arbitrarily. Bare boards get electrical test and dimensional checks; components get authenticity and date code checks; mechanical parts get dimensional checks against the drawing. Record results — pilot IQC data is the baseline against which mass production incoming quality is judged.

steps.exitTrigger: Assembly checklist confirmed and pilot build authorised
steps.entryQuestion: Does the EMS hold the complete pilot documentation set?
steps.exitQuestion: Has the EMS confirmed process readiness including stencil, profile and test fixture?
steps.whatToDo: Create the pilot assembly QC record and confirm the EMS has the complete pack and has confirmed process readiness.
steps.guidelines: Confirm documentation, materials, stencil, reflow profile and test arrangements are all in place. At pilot the EMS is also proving their process, so agree what data they will capture: first pass yield, defect types, cycle time. That data is what makes the mass production quotation and capacity plan credible.

steps.exitTrigger: Complete pilot package cross-checked and dispatched
steps.entryQuestion: Is every file and material verified at the pilot revision?
steps.exitQuestion: Is every dispatched item at the same released revision?
steps.whatToDo: Check the pack being sent against the released revision list before the pilot build starts.
steps.guidelines: Final verification and dispatch as at prototype, with a written record of what was sent and when. At pilot volume the cost of a revision mismatch scales with the build quantity, which makes this check proportionally more valuable than it was at prototype.

steps.exitTrigger: Pilot boards received with yield and defect data
steps.entryQuestion: Have AOI, X-ray and first pass yield data all been captured?
steps.exitQuestion: What was first pass yield, and what were the dominant defect modes?
steps.whatToDo: Record pilot assembly results: yield, AOI and X-ray findings, and the dominant defect mode with its count.
steps.guidelines: Receive with the yield and defect data, not just the boards. First pass yield and the dominant defect modes are what determine whether the design and process are ready for mass production. A pilot that produces working boards but no data has told you almost nothing about scalability. Feed defect modes back into DFM and the assembly instruction.

steps.exitTrigger: Firmware flashed and all boards verified with results recorded
steps.entryQuestion: Is the production flashing procedure being followed as written?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the documented procedure work at volume without firmware support?
steps.whatToDo: Record the pilot flashing run: version, hash, cycle time per unit and the failure rate at the station.
steps.guidelines: Run the documented flashing procedure exactly as written and note every point where the operator needed help — those are the gaps that will produce errors at mass production volume. Verify the git hash on every unit and record results per serial number. Measure the time per unit, since flashing time becomes a real constraint at volume.

steps.exitTrigger: Reliability testing complete on the pilot sample
steps.entryQuestion: Is the reliability test plan defined for pilot sample size?
steps.exitQuestion: Do results at pilot volume match what the prototype units showed?
steps.whatToDo: Record pilot reliability results with measured values and the hours each unit ran.
steps.guidelines: Test a defined sample against the reliability parameters. The value at pilot is variation: units built by a real process vary in ways prototype units assembled with care do not. Compare the spread against the prototype results and investigate any unit that behaves differently rather than averaging it away.

steps.exitTrigger: Functional testing complete across the pilot build
steps.entryQuestion: Is the functional test procedure repeatable by a line operator?
steps.exitQuestion: Is the test repeatable, and what is the test time per unit?
steps.whatToDo: Record pilot functional results and, critically, the test repeatability — is the procedure repeatable by a line operator?
steps.guidelines: Run functional test across the build using the production procedure and fixture. Two things are being validated here: the units, and the test itself. Measure test time per unit and check the procedure is repeatable between operators — a test that depends on operator judgement will not hold at mass production volume.

steps.exitTrigger: All pilot issues logged, dispositioned and closed
steps.entryQuestion: Are pilot issues being logged in the same tracker discipline as prototype?
steps.exitQuestion: Is any issue recurring from the prototype build, and was it genuinely closed?
steps.whatToDo: Log every pilot non-conformance, including the ones resolved on the line. Those are the ones that reveal the process problem.
steps.guidelines: Log pilot issues with the same discipline as prototype, and check specifically for recurrence — an issue that reappears after being marked closed was not root-caused, only worked around. Recurrence at pilot means it will recur at mass production volume, where the cost is multiplied by the batch.

steps.exitTrigger: Pilot field trial complete with results analysed
steps.entryQuestion: Are trial sites, duration and success criteria agreed?
steps.exitQuestion: Did any failure mode appear in the field that in-house testing did not predict?
steps.whatToDo: Record the pilot field trial against the agreed success criteria.
steps.guidelines: Deploy pilot units across a range of real conditions rather than one favourable site. The purpose is to find what in-house testing cannot reproduce — marginal network coverage, temperature extremes, unusual power quality, unexpected user behaviour. Any failure mode found here that testing did not predict indicates a gap in the test parameters, and that gap should be closed before mass production.

steps.step: Audit Checklist update — pilot build evidence
steps.exitTrigger: Pilot rows populated with build, yield and quality evidence
steps.entryQuestion: Are pilot build records, yield figures and non-conformances captured?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the checklist reflect what the pilot build actually produced rather than what was planned?
steps.whatToDo: Update the pilot rows with actual yield and every non-conformance raised. A pilot reporting only successes has not been measured.
steps.guidelines: Record actual yield and every non-conformance raised, including those resolved on the line. A pilot that reports only successes has not been measured; the deviations are the reason the pilot exists and are the input to the mass-production readiness decision.

steps.exitTrigger: Production handover package assembled and accepted by manufacturing
steps.entryQuestion: Is every document production needs present, current and consistent?
steps.exitQuestion: Has manufacturing confirmed they can build from this package without engineering support?
steps.whatToDo: Create the manufacturing sheet: quantities, stages, dates and the exact point at which responsibility passes to the EMS.
steps.guidelines: Assemble the complete package: fabrication files, multilevel BOM with approved sources, assembly documentation, test procedures and criteria, firmware and flashing procedure, packaging and labelling specifications, and quality criteria. The acceptance test is whether manufacturing can build from it unaided — a package that requires engineering support to interpret has not been handed over, only transmitted.

steps.entryTrigger: Test procedures defined and production volume known
steps.exitTrigger: Fixture requirements defined with specifications
steps.entryQuestion: What fixtures does production need for assembly, test and programming?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every test that must run at volume have a fixture defined for it?
steps.whatToDo: Create the production SOP and define the fixture requirements: what production needs for assembly, test and programming, with specifications.
steps.guidelines: Define the fixtures production needs: test fixtures with probe positions from the Net Accessibility register, programming fixtures, assembly jigs, and any go/no-go gauges. Size fixture count against takt time — one fixture becomes the line bottleneck at volume. Specify how the fixture connects and, critically, that it does not bypass the insulation being tested during safety test.

steps.exitTrigger: Fixture plan reviewed with test coverage confirmed
steps.entryQuestion: Do the fixtures give the test coverage the parameters require?
steps.exitQuestion: Does probe access match the test point strategy, and is throughput adequate?
steps.whatToDo: Review the fixture plan against the test coverage the parameters require, and confirm probe access matches the layout as built.
steps.guidelines: Review probe positions against the test point strategy and the Net Accessibility register — this is where a test point omitted at layout finally becomes visible as a coverage gap, and by then the only remedy is a partial test or a board change. Check throughput against production rate and confirm the fixture does not compromise the safety tests it participates in.

steps.exitTrigger: Fixture plan released and fixtures ordered
steps.entryQuestion: Are fixture specifications complete enough to build or procure against?
steps.exitQuestion: Will the fixtures be available and proven before production starts?
steps.whatToDo: Release the fixture plan and confirm the fixtures will be available before the first production run, not during it.
steps.guidelines: Release the specifications and order or build against them, allowing time for fixture debug — fixtures rarely work correctly first time and their debug is on the critical path to production start. Plan for calibration and periodic verification, since a drifting fixture passes bad units silently, which is worse than failing good ones.

steps.entryTrigger: Pilot validated and any pilot findings incorporated
steps.exitTrigger: Final enclosure design frozen for tooling
steps.entryQuestion: Are all pilot enclosure findings incorporated and the design final for tooling?
steps.exitQuestion: Is this design final, given that changes after tool cut cost weeks and tooling money?
steps.whatToDo: Release the final enclosure manufacturing drawings against the tool that will be cut.
steps.guidelines: Incorporate pilot findings and freeze. This is the last free change — after tool cut, modifications cost tooling money and weeks of schedule, and some changes are simply not possible in cut steel. Confirm all fit checks pass with pilot-representative parts, and confirm hardware is at the matching board revision.

steps.exitTrigger: DFMA report issued with findings and cost impacts quantified
steps.entryQuestion: Has the complete product been assessed for manufacturability and assembly at volume?
steps.exitQuestion: Are part count, assembly time and process complexity all justified at production volume?
steps.whatToDo: Create the DFMA report: part count against theoretical minimum, handling and insertion difficulty, assembly time and cost per part.
steps.guidelines: Assess the complete product at production volume: part count, assembly operations, orientation changes, fastener count, process steps and cycle time. Quantify the cost impact of each finding, because at volume a fifteen-second assembly saving is a real number. Findings that are not economic to change now inform the next generation and belong in the design learnings.

steps.exitTrigger: MFA report issued with line balance and bottlenecks identified
steps.entryQuestion: Has the manufacturing and assembly flow been analysed end to end?
steps.exitQuestion: Where is the bottleneck, and does the line balance meet the required rate?
steps.whatToDo: Create the MFA report: every station, its cycle time, yield and staffing, and name the bottleneck with a number beside it.
steps.guidelines: Analyse the full flow from incoming material to packed finished goods: station sequence, cycle time per station, line balance, material presentation, WIP buffers. Identify the bottleneck explicitly, because that is the only station whose improvement changes throughput. Include test and programming stations, which are frequently the constraint and are frequently omitted from the analysis.

steps.exitTrigger: Candidate vendors identified and evaluated against the standard form
steps.entryQuestion: Which vendors have proven capability in this process, material and size class?
steps.exitQuestion: Do they have the tonnage, the material experience and the quality system required?
steps.whatToDo: Create the vendor SAR and evaluate each candidate enclosure vendor on proven capability in this process, not on price alone.
steps.guidelines: Evaluate against the Vendor Evaluation Form: company details, works address, headcount, floor area, DGFT, MSMED, GST and PAN registration, customer list, five-year financials, and the technical services grid including DFMA capability. Visit where the tooling investment justifies it. Check machine tonnage against part size and material experience against the specified resin.

steps.exitTrigger: NDA executed with each shortlisted enclosure vendor
steps.entryQuestion: Is the NDA executed before any design data is shared?
steps.exitQuestion: Is tooling ownership addressed as well as confidentiality?
steps.whatToDo: Add the enclosure vendor NDA to the contracts pack, executed and dated before any drawing is shared.
steps.guidelines: Execute the NDA before sharing CAD, drawings or any design data — data shared ahead of the agreement is data with no protection, and quotation urgency is the usual reason it happens. Address tooling ownership explicitly in the same instrument: who owns the tool, where it is stored, and what happens on termination. Tooling ownership disputes are among the most damaging and most avoidable in this business.

steps.entryTrigger: Vendor evaluation complete and NDAs in place
steps.exitTrigger: Enclosure vendor selected and contracted
steps.entryQuestion: Are tooling cost, part price, lead time and capacity all quoted and comparable?
steps.exitQuestion: Are tooling ownership, part price at volume, and quality criteria all agreed in writing?
steps.whatToDo: Create the purchase agreement: price, tooling ownership, lead time, quality terms and what happens when a batch fails.
steps.guidelines: Negotiate tooling cost, part price at the committed volume, tooling lead time, sample submission schedule and quality acceptance criteria. Compare quotes on total cost across the expected volume rather than tooling cost alone — a cheaper tool with a higher part price loses quickly at volume. Confirm tooling ownership, storage location and the maintenance obligation in the contract.

steps.exitTrigger: DFMEA complete with high-RPN items mitigated
steps.entryQuestion: Have all potential design failure modes been identified and assessed?
steps.exitQuestion: Are all high-severity failure modes mitigated by design rather than by inspection?
steps.whatToDo: Create the DFMEA: every function, failure mode, effect, cause, control and RPN. Severity is never reduced by an action — only occurrence and detection can move.
steps.guidelines: Work through potential design failure modes with severity, occurrence and detection ratings. Focus on high-severity items regardless of their RPN — a rare failure with severe consequence deserves design mitigation, not a detection control. Mitigate by design where possible; relying on inspection to catch a design weakness transfers the problem to production and does not solve it.

steps.exitTrigger: PFMEA complete with process controls defined
steps.entryQuestion: Have all potential process failure modes been identified?
steps.exitQuestion: Does every high-risk process step have a control, and is that control verifiable?
steps.whatToDo: Create the PFMEA: every process step, what can go wrong, the prevention control and the detection control. Every high-risk step needs a control plan entry.
steps.guidelines: Work through the process step by step for what can go wrong: wrong part, wrong orientation, missed operation, out-of-spec process parameter. Define a control for each high-risk step and make the control verifiable — a control nobody can audit is an intention. Poka-yoke beats inspection wherever it is achievable, because it removes the failure mode rather than detecting it.

steps.entryTrigger: Final BOM released and volumes known
steps.exitTrigger: BOM vendors identified and evaluated
steps.entryQuestion: Which suppliers can support the required volume and lead time reliably?
steps.exitQuestion: Are single-source parts identified, and does each have a mitigation?
steps.whatToDo: Create the BOM RFQ and evaluate suppliers on volume support, lead time reliability and their handling of single-source lines.
steps.guidelines: Evaluate suppliers for the major BOM lines on capacity, lead time, financial stability and quality history. Identify every single-source part and put a mitigation against each — a second source, a buffer stock, or a documented accepted risk. Single-source parts without mitigation are the most common cause of production stoppage and the most predictable.

steps.exitTrigger: NDA executed with each shortlisted BOM vendor
steps.entryQuestion: Is the NDA executed before design data or volume forecasts are shared?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the agreement cover volume forecasts and design data, not just technical drawings?
steps.whatToDo: Add the BOM vendor NDA to the contracts pack, executed before the BOM is shared.
steps.guidelines: Execute NDAs before sharing the BOM, volume forecasts or design data. Volume forecasts are commercially sensitive in their own right and are frequently shared casually during quotation. Where the client's IP is involved, confirm the agreement permits onward disclosure to suppliers at all — some client agreements do not.

steps.entryTrigger: Vendor evaluation complete and NDAs in place
steps.exitTrigger: BOM vendors contracted with pricing and terms agreed
steps.entryQuestion: Are prices, lead times and minimum order quantities agreed at production volume?
steps.exitQuestion: Does the negotiated BOM cost meet the target COGS?
steps.whatToDo: Add the negotiated BOM vendor terms: price breaks, minimum order quantity, lead time and the shortage escalation route.
steps.guidelines: Negotiate price, lead time, minimum order quantity and payment terms at production volume, and secure allocation on constrained parts. Reconcile the negotiated total against the target COGS and report any variance to the project rather than absorbing it — a COGS overrun discovered at first invoice is a commercial problem that engineering could have helped solve earlier.

steps.entryTrigger: Production handover package complete and volumes known
steps.exitTrigger: EMS selected, contracted and onboarded with the full package
steps.entryQuestion: Does the EMS have the capability, capacity and quality system for this product at volume?
steps.exitQuestion: Have they demonstrated capability on this product, not just claimed it in general?
steps.whatToDo: Create the EMS audit checklist for the production partner and complete it on site, not over email.
steps.guidelines: Select on demonstrated capability for this product's process requirements at this volume, using the pilot data as evidence where the pilot assembler is a candidate. Onboard with the full handover package and confirm they can execute every documented process. Agree quality criteria, reporting cadence and escalation route before production starts, not after the first quality problem.
